subtopic: FRASER VALLEY RELIEF AND REHABILITATION COMMISSION

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FRASER VALLEY RELIEF AND REHABILITATION COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I informed the house in connection with the Fraser valley floods that it was the intention of the government to appoint a commission to have supervision over the entire situation, which commission would have on it a repre-

Flood Relief in British Columbia
sentative of the government of British Columbia and a representative of the federal government. I am happy to say that the federal government has been fortunate enough to obtain the services of Major General B. M. Hoffmeister as our representative. Hon. members will recall that General Hoffmeister was the officer appointed to command the Pacific forces at the time of the Japanese war. General Hoffmeister will be on loan from the H. B. MacMillan Company, of which he is the vice-president.
I am also happy to announce that Hon. Eric Hamber, former lieutenant governor of British Columbia, has agreed to act on the commission as the representative of the government of British Columbia. These two gentlemen will work together as representatives of our respective governments, and will have the opportunity of communicating directly with the ministers of both governments.
The federal representative on the commission will report to the Minister of Finance, but he will also have direct access to all departments of the federal government. The exact duties of the commission will be outlined more definitely later on.
In connection with the services of the navy, army and air force, General Hoffmeister will be available for consultations with Colonel Snow, commander of the Vancouver area of the Canadian Army, who, under direction from the Minister of National Defence, and with the authority of the provincial government, has been acting as co-ordinator of the agencies fighting the flood. Colonel Snow will remain the military officer in charge, responsible in the ordinary way to the military authorities and to the Minister of National Defence.
Just before coming into the house I received a telegram from Building Products Limited of Montreal, which company apparently has noticed that a commission was being established. This telegram is addressed to the Fraser valley relief and rehabilitation commission. That is the name that was suggested for the commission. It is sent in care of myself and is as follows:
If material required will be happy to donate five carloads of our roofing and siding products to Fraser Valley relief. All freight charges paid by us to destination.
Building Products Ltd.
I should like to express the thanks of the government to Building Products Limited. Their patriotic example is one which, in all probability, will be followed by many other industrial concerns in our country, and if so, such action will be deeply appreciated.
rMr. Mackenzie King.]

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: SUBSIDY ON BUTTER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUBSIDY ON BUTTER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: May I say a word on a related subject? I was informed the day before yesterday that washouts caused by the recent heavy floods had cut off the rail shipments of butter to British Columbia from the prairie provinces, the usual source of butter supplies for that province. Available stocks of butter in British Columbia, we were informed, were inadequate to meet the requirements of hospitals and many other high-rating claimants. It was suggested that the ceiling should be raised to provide for the added cost of flying in the necessary supplies, but that seemed to be inadvisable, and in order to meet this emergency the wartime prices and trade board have been authorized to pay a subsidy up to six cents a pound, or the difference between the cost of air and rail transport, whichever is the lesser, on butter moved by air transport from Lethbridge, Calgary or Edmonton to the isolated areas of British Columbia. This will enable the British Columbia consumers to continue to obtain butter supplies at prices within the price ceiling regulations.

maintopic: SUBSIDY ON BUTTER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with reference to the announcement just made by the Prime Minister, and speaking as a member from British Columbia, I know I am correct when I say that all the residents of that province feel that no finer appointment could have been made than that of Major General Hoffmeister. I know that British Columbia will welcome that appointment.
In view of the report as to the extent of the damage amounting to over S30 million, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he can elaborate on the statement made yesterday with regard to the extension of financial assistance, and particularly whether he will indicate the basis on which the federal government proposes to extend that assistance -whether on a dollar for dollar basis, or more, or less.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUBSIDY ON BUTTER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
May I thank my hon. friend for what he has just said in reference to the appointment of General Hoffmeister. The house I know will feel the same way with respect to the appointment of the former lieutenant governor, Hon. Eric Hamber, who is the nominee of the government of British Columbia. One of the purposes in the appointment of the commission was to afford opportunity of conferring between the representatives of both governments on all matters of importance in relation to flood conditions, in order that the governments might be advised confidentially, before

Inquiries oj the Ministry
final decisions were reached, as to amounts of payments and the like. I should be glad to give my hon. friend the information he has just asked for, if I had the facts upon which to base it. The government has felt that it would be preferable to have the whole situation surveyed by these gentlemen in the first instance.
May I say that both the government of British Columbia and our government are in entire agreement about the wisdom of appointment of the commission and its personnel.

maintopic: SUBSIDY ON BUTTER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with reference to the statement which the Prime Minister made yesterday and the statement he has made today, may I say that the term "Fraser river relief and rehabilitation commission" has been used several times. Will the Prime Minister give the house an assurance that the financial aid to be given to the province will be used to assist flood victims in all parts of the province and not in the Fraser river area alone?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUBSIDY ON BUTTER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: As I have said, one of the purposes of the appointment of the commission is to provide for a survey of the situation. Before the government reaches a decision as to the extent to which relief should be given, we should await the word we may receive from those who are in a position to advise in the matter.

maintopic: SUBSIDY ON BUTTER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I address a question to the Minister of Finance? In view of his statement as to the steps being taken to relieve the butter shortage in Vancouver, are any steps being taken to meet the grave danger of a milk shortage in Vancouver and other coast towns owing to the destruction of herds in the Fraser vallley, which is normally the source of supply of milk for that area?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUBSIDY ON BUTTER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA

maintopic: SUBSIDY ON BUTTER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Finance with reference to butter? When the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) left here and went to the distressed area, did he take his margarine with him or did he leave it in someone's keeping?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUBSIDY ON BUTTER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FARMERS-NET WORTH STATEMENT-INCOME TAX GUIDE AND ACCOUNT BOOK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Since confusion and misunderstanding have arisen in the minds of certain farmers with respect to the 1947 income tax forms and the Farmers' Income Tax Guide, will the minister please clarify the department's requirements with regard to use of these forms and guides.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCANN (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: FARMERS-NET WORTH STATEMENT-INCOME TAX GUIDE AND ACCOUNT BOOK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member I would first draw his attention to my statement of March 19, which appears in Hansard, page 2400, on the subject of the farmers' income tax form, and which deals particularly with the net worth statement appearing on this form. At that time I announced that the department had decided that farmers who report taxable income based on cash actually received and cash expenses actually paid out during the calendar year will not be required to fill out the net worth statement on the new 1947 prairie farmers' or farmers' income tax return. Farmers who report income on an accrual basis for tax purposes will be required to submit a statement of assets and liabilities as heretofore, or to complete the appropriate parts of the net worth statement.
It will be appreciated that under the terms of the Income War Tax Act where the department cannot obtain sufficient information by any other means it may require a further statement which in many instances may actually be "the net worth statement". This would apply, of course, to any year for which sufficient information Ls not available.
With respect to the farmers' income tax guide and account book which has been provided free to all farmers in Canada, I would like to point out that this book has two main purposes. The first one is to provide the Canadian farmer with a sample book for the puipose of recording his farm income and expenses in such a way as to facilitate the accurate completion of his income tax returns. The second is to answer general and specific questions which the department has found to be most common in its dealings with farmers.
I should add that the farmer is not obliged to use this accounting book. It has been provided free for his convenience and assistance. A farmer may keep, if he prefers, any other form of record which he finds more convenient.
The fact that the demand for these guides has resulted in over 700,000 copies being
Inquiries oj the Ministry

placed in the hands of Canadian farmers would indicate that they will be put to widespread use.

subtopic: FARMERS-NET WORTH STATEMENT-INCOME TAX GUIDE AND ACCOUNT BOOK
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question of the Minister of National Revenue. There is grave doubt about the situation as to farmers' income tax. My question is this: Suppose a farmer in his return for 1948 income fails to give the net worth statement, will he in 1949. if he changes his opinion, be denied the right then, to go on the accrual basis in the determination of his income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: FARMERS-NET WORTH STATEMENT-INCOME TAX GUIDE AND ACCOUNT BOOK
speechtext: I think not. I think he would be permitted to make the change from the cash basis to the accrual basis at that time.

subtopic: FARMERS-NET WORTH STATEMENT-INCOME TAX GUIDE AND ACCOUNT BOOK
speechtext: May I direct a supplementary question to the Minister of National Revenue? If the farmers take advantage of the permission that is now given not to fill in the form at the top of page 5, will it make any difference to or interfere with the farmer's right to claim to have his income spread over three years in case some years are good and some bad, as he has now under the act?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: FARMERS-NET WORTH STATEMENT-INCOME TAX GUIDE AND ACCOUNT BOOK
speechtext: I will take note of the question and give an answer tomorrow.

subtopic: FARMERS-NET WORTH STATEMENT-INCOME TAX GUIDE AND ACCOUNT BOOK
speechtext: I should like to direct a further question to the Minister of National Revenue arising out of the question asked by the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Breithaupt), and other questions of the same purport. Is it the intention eventually to have all farmers fill out the net worth statement? I do not mean this year or next year, but eventually.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: FARMERS-NET WORTH STATEMENT-INCOME TAX GUIDE AND ACCOUNT BOOK
speechtext: That is a matter of policy which has not yet been determined.

speechtext: I desire, Mr. Speaker, to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. In view of the indignation being expressed by some lumber and mining operators concerning their inability to purchase kerosene refrigerators, and in view of the fact that in some instances in British Columbia men are leaving camps not serviced with refrigeration to work in camps serviced with refrigeration, would the government give consideration to permitting the importation of kerosene refrigerators for purchase only for use in mining and lumber camps and isolated farms not serviced with electrical energy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: KEROSENE-OPERATED REFRIGERATORS FOR MINING AND LUMBER CAMPS AND ISOLATED FARMS
speechtext:
My hon. friend was good enough to give me notice of the question, and I have been able to look into the situation. I find that the emergency import control division is prepared to consider applications on an individual basis of essentiality in accordance with the hardship provisions of the order, and in fact a number of applications have been approved where supported by certificate from provincial health authorities indicating that it would be injurious to the health of workers if such equipment were not available. There have been a number of applications by companies and others representing that their camp was in an isolated area where electricity was not available and where supplies of provisions can be brought in only once a week, there being in such places 100 persons or more. These applications have been looked into and it has been found that, for example, what was asked for was an 8-foot refrigerator. Obviously it would be physically impossible to store perishables for 100 persons in a refrigerator of that size, and therefore the conclusion arrived at in a number of these cases was that the application was perhaps more for the benefit of senior hired help than for the mass of the employees.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: 309. Departmental administration, $1,096,287.

There are one or two matters, Mr. Chairman, which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister with a view to securing some information from him. The first has to do with representations that have been made to me by postmasters in revenue offices.
For these men and women there are no such things as minimum salaries or hours of employment, holidays or promotion. They render a great service to the people of the country as a whole; they receive their payment on a commission basis, and since they are not classified
as civil servants, they receive no pension. According to representations made to me, during the war they worked for a number of government departments without any remuneration, giving assistance in reporting enemy aliens, national registration, the foreign exchange control board, and generally making themselves useful in connection with various activities furthering the war effort. Having regard to the increase in the cost of living, and the surplus enjoyed by the post office department, what consideration has the government given to providing for a 25 per cent increase in rates as requested by these postmasters? Also, what if anything, is being done toward the establishment of a pension plan fop them?
Under the present deputy postmaster general, in common with hon. members in all parts of this house I have observed an attitude that I desire to commend. When matters are brought to the attention of the deputy postmaster genera], he has been most diligent in his endeavour to remove any cause of inconvenience. I think it only fair to say that; for after all, many of these officials are doing responsible, effective and efficient work. Too often we take for granted what they are doing, and fail to pass on to them and to those who work with them the commendation of the constituents whom we represent in parliament.
What consideration, if any, has been given during the year to the reduction of the postage rate from four cents to three cents, which was indicated last year as a possibility? The matter is one that I think deserves the consideration of the minister, and I feel that the committee should have an explanation with regard to it.
I want to join with the hon. member for Wentworth in the representations he made last evening on a matter to which he has made frequent reference. He asked that something be done to relieve the people from the present high postage rates on parcels sent to Britain to help the people over there. I know of two or three persons in my own constituency who during the last year have sent parcels, to the limit now allowed, to the parents of young men who served in the armed! forces of this country and whose acquaintance they made during the war. The minister has had this matter brought to his attention on previous occasions. I know he would have the support of Canadians everywhere were he to make provision to remove, as far as possible, the postage rates on parcels being sent to Great Britain by patriotic Canadians with a view to assisting .the people over there to get additional nutritional value in their diet.
Supply-Post Office

On previous occasions I have heard the arguments used in answer to this request. But if the minister could see the letters that one receives from men and women in the lower-income brackets who regard it as a patriotic duty to assist their kinsmen overseas, and who are prevented from being as generous as they otherwise would be because of the high transportation charges, some favourable consideration would be given to the matter. I ask the minister what he proposes to do about it. I know he will say that he realizes the conditions that exist, but that-there are administrative difficulties in the way. I say to him: remove those difficulties; give Canadians an opportunity to help their relatives and friends in Great Britain. When they are voluntarily sending parcels to assist people in another part of this commonwealth, it is difficult for them to understand why they must pay a postage rate which is as high or almost as high as the value of the things they are sending. The same argument, of course, applies to patriotic organizations who prepare bundles to assist destitute families in England and who find1 themselves penalized to a degree that seems scarcely justifiable.
I would like the minister to tell the committee also what is 'being done about the representations made by the rural mail couriers wherein they point out the unfairness of the present tender system, and urge that the present contract system by tender be discontinued and replaced by a contract system comparable with other similar postal services, under which a definite price would be determined for each individual route, subject to revaluation when made necessary by changes in mileage, number of boxes, and the like.
I shall not go into all the representations which have been made in that connection. The bonus system was merely a temporary arrangement to meet individual cases, though in some of those cases-and I have the records before me-there was an unusual spread as between various applicants operating similar routes. I do not know what would be the justification, but when one finds two routes approximately the same in length, with the bonus in one case greater than in the other, one wonders on what basis it was done.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Because the conditions were very different.
Mr. D1EFENBAKER: That may be true, but physical conditions are not always the reason for the difference in these payments.
Political conditions.

Certainly some of them seem hard to justify; they would indicate one basis for certain individuals and areas, and another for others. The minister says conditions are different. That explanation may cover the situation generally, but it is something which at the moment I would prefer not to discuss in too great detail. I do think the bonus system, being merely temporary, should be supplanted in accordance with the suggestions made by the rural mail couriers' association, whose representations are couched in reasonable and temperate language, and with a full realization not only of their position but also of their responsibility as servants of this country.
Finally I have one further question. In the appointments to fill vacancies, is the veterans' preference actually being carried out? I should like to know the number of appointments made during the past year, vacancies and replacements, and the number of men and women appointed who have the veteran qualification.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Last evening we discussed the question of revenue postmasters to a certain extent, but I am glad the hon. gentleman has raised1 the question again because I want, to make a more complete statement. We have been using an antiquated method of paying the postmasters, and in our view it is very unfair in many instances.
What method is the minister referring to?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Payments
based on revenue. When I came into the department-<1 do not say I was responsible for correcting this situation-there were revenue postmasters in what had become large centres of population, and as a result they were receiving much more than they should, though of course there were very few of those. There were some also who should have received more than they were getting. The method of paying postmasters according to the postage sold was not the best, because in certain post offices a great deal of work has to be done in addition to selling stamps. A post office may be a distribution centre for rural mail, or may distribute mail to other post offices, and in that case the work is much heavier. So we decided to change that system, and have been doing so since April 1. Of course it involves a great deal of work, and we cannot change it all at the same time.

What is the change?

Supply-Post Office

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
We are
putting them on straight salary according to the importance of their office. We are also taking it upon ourselves to see that their employees, if they need employees, are properly paid. We do not now leave this to the discretion of the postmaster, because sometimes they may pay a little less than they should, and we want the employees to be properly paid. There was a case in Saskatchewan in which an employee of a revenue post office was not receiving the minimum wage under provincial law. That employee, though working in the post office, was not directly employed by us. Such cases will not occur in future.
We have also received representations from many quarters asking us to extend the right of superannuation to these employees. We could not do that when they were paid according to the revenue received from the sale of postage, but now we have submitted to treasury board a plan under which those employees will be brought under superannuation.
What is the plan?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
They will
contribute a certain amount, as other civil service employees do, and those within a certain age will pay what is necessary in order to entitle them to superannuation under the act so that they may retire at the age of sixty-five and have something on which to live, like other civil service employees. In some cases postmasters have been in office for a long time and are quite old. They may be unable to do anything else, and too old properly to serve the public. In such cases it is very disagreeable to have to tell them they must give up their job to somebody else, without being able to offer them any superannuation. That is one reason for changing the method of payment.
The hon. gentleman spoke about the salaries we are paying. The salary varies, of course, according to the work done in the individual offices. I might add that this superannuation can apply only to postmasters whose offices have a revenue of at least $3,000, and in the case of such offices the salary, as determined at the moment, is to be $1,920.
How many post offices are in that position?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: There are 1,385 with a revenue of above $3,000. As yet we have not fixed a figure for post offices with a revenue of less than $3,000. We are studying the matter now, and it takes time to arrive at a definite conclusion.

What are the
alternative plans the minister is considering in reference to post offices with an income of less than $3,000?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
There are
some small post offices where the revenue is not $100, and it would be difficult to provide superannuation for a postmistress in charge of such a small office. We are working to see to what extent we can do this, but we cannot say exactly what we are going to do.
The hon. gentleman asked me about the three-cent and four-cent- rates of postage. In both cases there is a one cent tax. That is not charged by the Post Office Department, although the department benefits from any surplus. That tax could not be eliminated except by action of the government. Expenses have increased considerably. Salaries to our employees have been increased by $660, and we are paying more to the rural mail contractors, railway clerks, and so on. We could hardly recommend to the Minister of Finance that we return to the three cents and two cents postage when costs are what they are.
In the United States immediately after the war considerable pressure was put on the government to return to the pre-war postage rates of three cents and two cents, the same as we had before the war. The airmail rate was reduced from eight cents to five cents, and they reduced other rates. The result was disastrous. At the end of the year they had a deficit of $442 million, and the President sent a message to congress asking them to try to find some way to make up this deficit. If we reduced our rates in Canada it would mean a loss of revenue of between $11 million and $14 million in first-class letter rates. We are trying to improve service by providing all-up mail service on July 1 as an experiment. Through this service we shall be able to deliver mail in Canada just as quickly as though we were a small country only 150 or 200 miles long. It will be an experiment, but I am quite sure it will work. We have to admit that we are experimenting. We would not be able to recommend elimination of the one-cent tax.
Is the revenue from that one-cent tax shown under the heading of taxation, or does it go into the revenues of the Post Office Department?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
It all goes in the same pot. We return all our revenue to the consolidated revenue fund, and it is counted in any surplus there may be. It might be diverted to national revenue, but it all

Supply-Post Office
goes into the consolidated revenue fund and then we draw on that fund according to what is voted here.
Reference was made to the high postage rates on gift parcels to Great Britain. According to our figures, only five per cent of the British people are receiving gift parcels. We are not making any money out of these parcels, as we charge only for our out-of-pocket expenses. The largest parcel that can be sent is twenty pounds, but small parcels of five pounds or so are sent quite often. The cost on these parcels is high. The total postage is 85 cents, but we have to pay 38 cents for sea transportation and 27 cents to the British post office for handling and delivering there, which leaves us 20 cents as payment for transporting a parcel, say from the west to Halifax.
If the present rates were reduced it would mean that we would be paying a subsidy or making a donation to individuals instead of to the people as a whole.
As I say, only about five per cent of the British people receive gift parcels because they have friends or relatives here. We have the greatest sympathy for the people in England. I have friends there to whom I send parcels once in a while. I may say that my deputy minister is going to Britain in a few weeks to discuss certain matters, and this question of parcels will be one of them. It may be that the reduction could be made on the other side instead of here, and that would help the people who are sending parcels.
Has any request been made of the United Kingdom government that they forgo the charges they make for transmitting these parcels in Britain?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Yes, the
United Kingdom authorities have been asked to do that.
How do these rates compare with those charged on parcels for the troops during the war?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: During the war we did not have to pay the steamship companies anything for the distribution of these parcels, because it was done by the army.
The rate was quite low, was it not?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
It was twelve cents a pound, and on a twenty-pound parcel the rate was ten cents cheaper than our present rate.
As to the tender system, the hon. member for Lake Centre indicated that it might be dangerous to leave the fixing of the rates to

the department alone. Tenders have always been called for. Of course there will always be certain persons who are willing to accept a lower price because they are in a position to do it. Perhaps they are carrying merchandise as well as the mail, or carrying passengers. Some of them run taxis. If we attempted to fix a standard price there would have to be as many standard prices fixed as there are railway freight rates, because the routes vary greatly as to number of boxes, difficulties of the road, and so forth. One contractor might be getting on in years and be glad to carry the mail to earn a little money. Another man might be the father of a large family and would require more remuneration. . I am quite certain that if we fixed a rate the department itself would be the loser and very few people would gain by it.
During the war, because the cost of living was going up, we had to grant bonuses and supplements, but supplements were granted only on the merits of each individual case, where it was absolutely necessary to increase the amount. When we compare the number of cases in which supplements were granted with the number of cases in which it was necessary to ask for tenders because, for example, of the death of the contractor, we find that the proportion was 36 per cent in the one case and 39 per cent in the other. The tenders were about three per cent higher.
I could not say offhand just how many veterans we employed last year, but we make it a rule in the department to give the veterans the preference, and we go a long way to help the veteran. Many temporaries were taken on during the war and served in the department for five or six years; some were replaced as the veterans came back, but there are temporaries still in the service. I could get the figures my hon. friend asked for.
I wish the minister would.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I shall do that with pleasure.

I was unable to be present during all the discussion on postal matters, and perhaps the point I have in mind has already been dealt with. I wanted to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General one class of employees in the postal service who I think are worthy of the best possible consideration; I refer to the railway mail clerks. They have the hardest of hard work. Their hours are about the worst of any group in the civil service. The

Supply-Post Office
work is often exceedingly dangerous. It is wearing on the nerves, as we all know, and often these employees come to the verge of a complete breakdown. They have day runs, night runs-all kinds of runs except home runs; because their home life is completely broken into. Their facilities for getting meals are most inadequate. They have in their custody registered mail, and that tends to worry them. If something has not been done already for this class of employees, I trust that it will be done. I should also have mentioned that their work is done in a rush, because they have to be ready with the mail at each trainstop; they are on edge all the time. I would like to see these conditions recognized financially and otherwise by the department.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The railway post office employees are the highest paid class in the department, and whenever these positions become vacant, employees in other branches are glad to take them, because it is considered as a promotion.

I would like to have a state-men from the Postmaster General as to what his department has done in cutting down the rather top-heavy subsidy that has been paid for some time by the Post Office Department with respect to newspapers and periodicals in the second-class mailing group, where there is a mailing rate of one and a half cents a pound. This matter was taken up by me last year. At that time I had the support of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I am hoping that the minister will be able to make a statement indicating that some change has been made in the policy.
I want to remind the minister that last year I asked him a question as to how we stood financially with respect to the handling of newspapers and periodicals by the Post Office Department. In reply to my question he said that the loss in handling was estimated at $7,287,400 per annum. Even the Postmaster General must admit that a subsidy of that kind to people who I think could get along quite well without it makes quite a dent in the otherwise excellent service which his department can provide. Newspapers, which are the biggest recipients of the subsidy involved in the charge made for second-class mail matter- including newspapers, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says, which consistently decry subsidies for what I would call humanitarian purposes-are permitted to sell advertising up to fifty per cent of their total space and still remain within the second-class field. I think some change should be made in that regard. They definitely receive large revenues 5849-304
on the sale of these advertisements. On top of that they receive a subsidy which in effect amounts to approximately one-tenth of the minister's estimated revenues for the year just ended, 1947-48. That is quite a big contribution from the rest of the Canadian citizens to this one service which is handling and distributing second-class mail matter. The department, by efficient management, did have, according to the budget report and the estimates that are before us, in spite of this big concession, a revenue of approximately $8,010,000 in 1947-48. By requiring the newspapers to pay the exact cost of providing these services, the department could have had a revenue for the past year of some $15,300,000 net, as I calculate it.
I do not think the minister will quarrel with the way in which I have built up the figures to indicate that, had they paid their own way for all these services, the net revenue to the Post Office Department would have been over $15,000,000 instead of the present estimated one of $8,000,000. We would have almost doubled our net revenue had a different policy been implemented by the Post Office Department with respect to the charges on newspapers and periodicals. Had that been done perhaps the Postmaster General could have subsidized these relief parcels which have been mentioned by quite a number of hon. members in the house, food parcels for overseas, or he could have given a 25 per cent increase in pay to post office employees all across Canada instead of the timid increases which were mentioned last night by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
As a matter of fact I believe the minister has received representations almost annually from organized groups of letter carriers to the effect that second-class mail matter be handled by the corporations which send them out through postal channels. I hold in my hand a resolution from the federated association of letter carriers, the final paragraph of which reads as follows:
Be it resolved that the delivery of individual magazines, periodicals, newspapers, catalogues, et cetera, by letter carriers be discontinued, and that said magazines, newspapers, periodicals, catalogues, et cetera be delivered en masse to news depots or duly authorized agents appointed by the publishers of said magazines, newspapers, periodicals, catalogues, et cetera.
I appreciate the reason why the letter carriers take that stand. In my own city, when one gets off the pavement in the early spring of the year and on that South Saskatchewan gumbo, a pretty husky man or woman could get stuck with the load that these people carry when they go out on their routes. It seems to me that it is time the minister seriously contemplated a complete revision either
Supply-Post Ojjice

of the rates or of the service in connection with second-class mail matter. I would appreciate a word or two with respect to that general subject.
I listened attentively, but I must admit I did not hear the observation of the minister a while ago. I should like to know what he said. Sitting here I could not get it at all.

It is not very often that I have the opportunity of supporting suggestions made by the hon. member for Regina City, but this subject has been a kind of pet interest of mine. I would be much interested, in a matter of this kind, to hear the views of the Progressive Conservative party. This is a matter of great concern. It is a tangible way in which we might save a little of the taxpayers' money. If a change were made here we might cut some of the expenditures of government. Surely there should be some way in which we could rectify the situation.
I understand that we have to carry newspapers. I am all for the broadcasting of proper information to the public. I think everyone would be willing to carry, out of our revenues, a necessary service of this kind, but there should be some limit to it. Newspapers published in Montreal or Toronto, for instance, are carried all the way out to Vancouver. As a matter of fact my pet peeve against these papers has been that they carry very little actual news or factual material, and we could get along very well without them. In fact the publishers in Vancouver complain bitterly that Little Orphan Annie arrives out there via the Toronto Star Weekly or the Montreal Standard on Tuesday, three or four days ahead of the time that cartoon appears in their papers, and I do not think that is a fair practice. It is not fair to a good newspaper like the Vancouver Sun or the Vancouver Province, which rarely gets down to this part of the country except in the parliamentary reading room. This is just one more instance of all the people subsidizing the manufacturers of news in Ontario and Quebec.
I would ask the minister to give some explanation as to why there is not some limit in this matter. I hate to have the thought in my mind that there is some kind of intangible or subtle blackmail, as it were, perhaps unconscious, on the part of the newspapers. But the fact remains that neither the Liberal government nor the Conservative government when in power-and I doubt whether the C.C.F. would change this, although it would be interesting to hear what the attitude of the hon. member for Regina City is-has done anything
IMr. Probe.]
about the matter. It has always seemed to me that there was something that somebody was afraid to do anything about. I would be interested to hear the minister's explanation.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
First, in
answer to the hon. member for Brandon, I said that railway clerks in the post office were the highest paid employees in the department, and whenever a vacancy occurs there are always many other employees who wish to get into that branch. If they are successful they consider themselves promoted. I will not say why they like to travel, but I suppose they have good reasons.
As regards the deficit on newspapers and periodicals, which this year is $7,500,000, I admit it is a large amount, but the rates are fixed by parliament and are not under the jurisdiction of the Postmaster General. I admit that they are not reasonable, but they were created through the years when the newspapers were not of their present bulk of 30, 40 or 50 pages.
When was the act first passed?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I do not remember offhand.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: None of us were here.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: In 1932, I am informed. Today the newspapers are heavy. We gave them the privilege of paying one cent and something-
One cent and a half per pound.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
That is right, for the full poundage of the newspaper, provided they did not publish more than 50 per cent of advertising. I maintain that in the department we are very fair, because, although the law provides that it shall be 50 per cent, it is sometimes difficult to determine a just pro rata, and we start to count at 54 per cent instead of 50 per cent.
I understand that when this arrangement was established it was a good thing for the people receiving newspapers, but today there is a change. For one thing, the radio provides people in the country with a good deal of news, and the different political parties have since begun to broadcast and are teaching many things to certain provinces-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
with results. I must admit, in certain cases. There is also the privilege of sending free the speeches that are made in this house, which is taken advan-

Supply-Post Office
tage of to a large extent. As I say, I admit that the deficit of $7,500,000 on newspapers is too high.
That is right.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We are looking into the question. As a matter of fact, a newspaper representative came to us and made a certain offer which I will not disclose now since we are studying it at the moment. The deficit attributable to the dailies is only $1,500,000, the other $6 million being created by other publications and magazines. In Canada we are in a rather peculiar position. We receive many more American magazines than we ourselves deliver to the United States, and this of course accounts for a certain part of. the deficit.
You had better start saving foreign exchange.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
There are
international regulations and they cannot be changed by one party for a particular reason without reference to the bulk of the regulations. Some years ago, before my time, we succeeded in getting American publishers to ship to Toronto their publications for Canadian distribution. Those that are to be distributed in Canada are mailed here, so that at least we have a certain revenue in that direction, whereas if they were mailed in New York or some other city in the United States we would lose a larger amount than we do.
The question is a delicate one. Of course people must realize that if the newspapers pay $1,500,000 more the cost of newspapers will be advanced, and instead of two cents it will be five cents for most newspapers. That is coming anyhow.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: They are all five cents now.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The question is being studied along with many other matters in the department, and I may say that we are quite studious.

Can the minister tell the committee whether or not a design has yet been selected for the commemorative stamp to be issued on the occasion of the Halifax bicentenary in 1949, and also what the denomination of that stamp will be?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: A design is being studied by different artists, but one has not yet been definitely chosen. The stamp will be a four-cent stamp.

I understand that the United States intend to issue a special stamp in August to commemorate the centen-.ory of peace with Canada. Does the minister, 5849-304J
as Postmaster General, intend to reciprocate the decision made by the United States and have a similar type of stamp issued by Canada?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, any question about philately is always a delicate one. Indeed, there are many more philatelists in the world than I ever dreamed of before I became Postmaster General.
They bring in a lot of profit, too.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Yes; but in the long run, if we granted all their requests, our stamps would be depreciated from the philatelists' point of view. Our stamps have a high value in the world of philately, for the reason that we do not make too many issues. We wait until there is a very good reason.
The stamp commemorating the Niagara bridge, which has been referred to as being associated with the centenary of peace, is not exact from the historical point of view, because peace was signed between Canada and the United States in 1815, whereas the bridge was opened to the public 100 years ago. There has been pressure to have a stamp commemorating the opening of the bridge. This is a private bridge, and it would be helping a private organization in its publicity. I was not Postmater General at the time, but a few years ago the city of Vancouver celebrated its centenary. Many people are of the opinion that we should have issued a stamp on that occasion, and I would suggest that to issue a stamp commemorating the centenary of the erection of this bridge, in view of the fact that we did not issue one to mark the foundation of Vancouver, would not be fail'. Of course the United States issue many more stamps than we do, but their stamps have not the same value from the philatelic point of view.
Does this all add up to the fact that, after so many words, the Postmaster General does not intend to issue such a stamp?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I must say it was a diplomatic way of saying no.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to ask the Postmaster General what are the regulations and the practice with respect to stamp meters. Some letters are put out metered without anything else on the letter but the stamp itself. But sometimes there are little slogans or designs that go along with the meter. I have in my hand an interesting one that was given to me a little while ago. It was put out on meter number 140,287. The letter was mailed at Montreal on March 30, 1948. The amount
Supply-Post Office

of postage paid was four cents. The slogan that is printed as part of the cancellation stamp reads as follows: "Free enterprise means good living. Keep it alive."

There
should be more of that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I was fairly sure that that slogan would receive endorsement in most parts of this house, but the enthusiasm shown by my hon. friend simply supports my contention that it is a political slogan.
The hon. member just made it up.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I did not make it up at all. It is stamped on the letter by the post office metering machine.

The hon. member is
making it a slogan, though.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is stamped on the letter.
Why does the hon. member not adopt it?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is it the policy of the Post Office Department to put out slogans from time to time? If so, I should like to offer some suggestions. For instance, next week, how about "Humanity first"; or "Make this your Canada"; or "Production for use and not for profit"? Or maybe my friends to my right have some slogans to suggest.
They will speak for themselves.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Calgary West gave an interesting one: "Yale, Yale, the gang's all here I"
This may be amusing, Mr. Chairman, but it is also serious. I should like to know just where the line is drawn in the matter of the slogans that go with these meters. Is the slogan put into the meter which a firm may rent from the post office, or may a firm rent one of these meters and put in any slogan it wishes? If the latter, I still think that either some line should be drawn or we down at Woodsworth House should be allowed to rent a meter and put in any slogan we wish to use.
Where is Woodsworth House?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Woodsworth House is the C.C.F. national office at 301 Metcalfe street, here ini Ottawa.
That is where they sing the Red Flag.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Not at all. WTien a slogan is put out in this way, it gives the people who receive it the impression that there is something official about it. I should be glad to have the Postmaster General's comments on this matter.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: May I have the envelope to which the hon. member referred?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes; I shall be glad to send it over to the Postmaster General.

Perhaps when the Postmaster General is answering the question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre he will also explain why the post office favour the use of postal meters. It is because of the time saved to the employees, and also the splendid service given by free enterprise and those who are willing to 'buy these meters at a fairly substantial amount, paying $100 in advance. Instead of going in and buying a few stamps at a time and taking up the time of the vendor, they buy $100 worth at a time, get a receipt, and their register is shown at that amount. They continue to use it day after day until they use up that amount; then they go back for a further large amount, and their money is deposited with the Post Office Department. I think it is a splendid method of saving time both for the employer and for the Post Office Department. With regard to slogans, I may say that I use one of these machines and I have a slogan. I advertise that great Atlantic port, Halifax. The stamp is marked, "Halifax", and underneath it "That great Atlantic port". I also speak of a fine brand of clothes and carry a slogan about them, but I have a slogan too which helps Halifax.
Isnor's "Fit-U clothes".

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
We allow
corporations to rent or buy meters, and our duty is to see that we are not defrauded of our revenue in any way. We see to that. Some of the corporations like to have a motto like this one, "Free enterprise means good living; keep it alive." Others would like some other one. As long as those mottoes are not indecent or insulting,- and so on, we have no objection.
If they insult your intelligence, is that all right?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Question.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Intelligence is so different in different people that I can see why, for instance, a son-in-law does not agree with his mother-in-law. But I must

Supply-Post Office
tell the hon. gentlemen that we also have slogans which are asked for at different times. We are scribblers to a certain extent in the department. Now that this has come up, I must admit that this week a certain political party in Quebec asked to have this slogan put on their letters: "Vote Liberal."
Right on the envelope?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Much to my disappointment I had to say no; I refused to allow it.

You might insult their
intelligence.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes. Of course, these meters serve a useful purpose. They save a great deal of money to people who send out a large number of letters, having regard to the amount of labour involved. Stamps do not have to be put on the letters. If even the Progressive Conservative party want to use a meter and put on something which is decent, and which is according to their orthodox thinking-if it can be called orthodox-we have no objection to it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just in order to have the regulation clear, do I understand that when the Post Office Department rents a meter -and incidentally I support the statement made by the senior member for Halifax that this is a good idea-to organizations or corporations, they must submit a proposed slogan to the department in all cases, or are they free to put in anything they wish?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: They are free to put in whatever they want to, but if it so happens that we do not want it, it would be too bad for the organization that is submitting something which we cannot permit.
Does the department have to pass on these slogans before they are accepted or put into the machine?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
No. But if
something indecent were to come out, we would intervene.
I am not quite clear on this. I understood the Postmaster General to say that he turned down a request from his own province to vote Liberal.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: It was for a slug.
Was it because that was an indecent statement to go on the letter that the request was turned down?
It was too political; that is all.

I think we should have this matter clarified. I understood the minister to suggest that if the Progressive Conservative party wanted a slogan, it would be quite in order, but that he had to turn down a similar request from his own party in Quebec. I think the idea of boosting Halifax or Vancouver or Edmonton is quite worthy-

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We allow those things.
And I think they are quite worthy.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: But when an election is taking place in a province or in Canada it would be improper for the Postmaster General to permit anything which would refer to one party as against another.

Elections are being fought, or are about to be fought, and it seems to me hardly the thing to have business firms and other organizations carry on political activity by putting in a plug for free enterprise, or trying to discredit views they do not support, at the same time creating the impression that this is the official party of the government of Canada, which at the moment happens to be a Liberal government. In a few years we may have a C.C.F. government, and it would be hardly cricket for any political party in power to sanction the use of slogans on these meters in support of one political party and in an attempt to discredit others. So I think this policy should be reviewed by the Postmaster General.

I have just one question, which may have been cleared up, on the matter of this reduced rate on air mail. Suppose an airmail letter is sent to my own city of Portage la Prairie, for instance, where the planes do not land. That letter would be taken to Winnipeg and sent by train to Portage la Prairie. Would the same rate apply?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes.
Even though it was not taken all the way by air mail?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The public need not worry about that. We will send the mail by plane at the same price wherever we can gain time.

I should like to ask one or two questions; I have looked through Hansard and have not seen them dealt with, though I have been out of the chamber for some time today. I am not clear as to what post offices are to come under the civil service. I am very much interested in that question. I have objected strenuously, as have many of
Supply-Post Office

my constituents, to men who were operating quite successful companies and receiving fair remuneration also acting as postmasters, spending a great deal of time away from the post office and letting their wives or some other employees do the work for a very small remuneration. So I should like the minister to tell us exactly what type of post office is coming under the civil service.
Then the Department of Labour informs me that employees of a rural postmaster come within the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I should like to ask what the Post Office Department does to see that rural postmasters comply with dominion laws.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Post offices with revenue of $3,000 and up will now come under the civil service, and these postmasters are asked to spend all their time at that job. It has not been decided as yet whether post offices with revenue of less than $3,000 will come under the civil service. As to the unemployment insurance, this is a matter which must be looked after by the contractor.
The Postmaster General did not quite get my question. I was referring to employees of rural postmasters working in post offices.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The arrangement is similar.

The Canadian National Railways, operating about sixty per cent of the railway mileage in Canada and employing about sixty per cent of the railway personnel, has never been able to get its full share of the post office business. Could the Postmaster General report what percentage of the amount paid out last year went to the Canadian National and what percentage to the Canadian Pacific, and could he also tell us what prospect the Canadian National has of getting its sixty per cent share as soon as possible?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We do not distribute the postal bags according to the miles served by the two railways. We send the mail by whichever railway is more convenient. I am not sure, but it may happen that the Canadian Pacific passes through an older section of the country, and must receive a little more. I do not know exactly; I have never calculated who gets the larger share.

The Canadian National provides equally good service between Winnipeg and Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, and Montreal and Vancouver; and if the Canadian Pacific is getting more than its fair

share of the revenue I should imagine it would be easy to divert some of that mail in order to ensure that each company gets its fair share.
They never arrive on time.
My hon. friend had better not say that in any part of Canada served by the Canadian National, because they are very proud of the service they receive.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Some officials of the Canadian National have complained in this connection. We have asked them to come and look at the figures, and if they were ill treated we would see what could be done.
Has the minister the percentages paid the two companies?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: They are paid according to the work done, and the work is given to whichever company serves the greatest population.
If the minister would just give us the percentage of the revenue going to each company we could see the position.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Last year the Canadian Pacific were paid $4,177,000, and the Canadian National, $3.756,000.
I do not think that is satisfactory. In view of the fact that the Canadian National has more mileage and more employees, there really is no justification-

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: That is not the point. The point is whether they serve as large a population.

They both serve
Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal and the larger centres, so that I think the time has come when our publicly owned railway should get at least fifty per cent of the amount .the Post Office Department pays the railway companies in Canada.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
We have
asked the officials of the Canadian National to discuss this matter with us, but so far they have not come. We want to serve the people in the best way possible. We do not care whether it is done by the Canadian National or by the Canadian Pacific. As a member of parliament, I can appreciate that the more we can give the Canadian National, the more it will benefit that railway, which badly needs additional revenue. It goes according to the number of bags collected on the way and the number sent from one city to another.

Supply-Post Office
We cannot discuss the matter very well here, because we have asked those interested to discuss it with us and so far they have not done so.

I have brought up this point year after year. If the officials of the Canadian National have not come this year I am sure it is not because they have not been concerned about getting some adjustment. When those officials have been before committees of this parliament they have told us they have not been satisfied with the percentage of the revenue they have been getting and that they have been negotiating for a larger percentage. As a taxpayer in Canada, the Postmaster General is concerned about the financial position of his own railway; and I think it is not unreasonable to ask that the Canadian National, our own railway, should get at least fifty per cent of the revenue. I am not asking that we should discontinue mail service to Canadian Pacific points; but the Canadian National has good trains between Toronto and Winnipeg, Winnipeg and Vancouver, Montreal and Vancouver, and so on, and there is no reason why we could not give the Canadian National more money.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman is making a point on a question which is very difficult, involving a great deal of study, and which I cannot answer at the moment. We did the reasonable thing; we asked the officials of the Canadian National to discuss this matter with us, and we are waiting for them.

I want to ask the minister a further question about this tax that has been put on the people who use the post office savings department. I should like to ask why the department thought it necessary to impose this tax. This service has been given for a great number of years, and people have been permitted to withdraw money from the postal savings bank without this tax being imposed. Now all of a sudden the Post Office Department decides that it should tax at the same rate as the chartered bank. Why was it deemed necessary? Was it to increase revenue? If so, how much increased revenue has been obtained?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
The savings bank is not a paying proposition, because we lose money in the sense that we give service free. The bank is intended to be exclusively a savings bank, and it is used by many people in far-off places or by foreigners who have confidence in the Canadian government, whatever it may be, and deposit their money there. However, it has been found that certain people
are using their post office savings accounts as checking accounts. We think it reasonable that they should pay the same tax that is imposed on anyone who goes to a bank and draws a cheque.
Was it done to obtain increased revenue or to discourage people from using their accounts?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: It was done to discourage people from using this bank as an ordinary commercial bank instead of as a savings bank.

I can see the force of the minister's argument if this tax were imposed only on people who are travelling and use the post office savings bank as a convenience, but I do not think his argument is valid when applied to people in remote places where there is no bank. He is penalizing those who live in outlying districts in order to discourage people from using this bank. It seems to me that in doing this the Post Office Department is forcing people to use the chartered banks. The post office savings bank should be for the convenience of people, particularly those in outlying districts who have not access to chartered banks. I think the revenue the minister will get will be negligible, while the service that could be rendered is considerable. We have got along all these years without imposing this tax, and I do not think we should start to do it when the post office revenue is up so high. It certainly cannot be for revenue, and the only conclusion one can come to is that this is being done to discourage the people from using this service. If that is true, then the proper thing to do would be to close up the service entirely. Goodness knows, we have enough taxes nowadays without having any new ones.

I was speaking the other day about changes in mail services where the railroad provides service only three times a week, but I have another matter I should like to bring up now. This concerns a community which is served partly by bus and partly by rail. The patrons have requested that the mail be carried every day by bus because there is a daily service. I wrote to the minister on behalf of the people of Williams Lake on December 8. I had a reply on December 15 saying that careful inquiry would be made into the matter, but I have heard nothing since that time. From conversation with officials of the department, I understand that the whole question of carrying mail by bus is being investigated. Is the minister in a position to say anything about it today?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Any material from another country is supposed to be censored by the customs department. I know this, because when I was an attorney I had to come and discuss certain points with the officials here concerning exactly what the hon. member for Lake Centre has brought up. If it is domestic we rely, and rightly so, upon the attorneys general of the different provinces. There is a tendency to impose upon the Postmaster General the duties of the Attorney General of Canada, something that I do not like myself. The attorney general is the one to say what is criminal or what should be prohibited. Under the postal regulations we have the right to stop immoral books whenever we find them.
Recently I received protests in connection with the importation of a book which has been sold in large numbers in the United States. I understand that 200,000 copies have been sold at $7 or $8 each. This book is supposed to be immoral because it relates to sex.
It is a best seller in the United States.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I am going to read this book myself, and then I am going to ask somebody else to read it so that I shall not be the only one to pass an opinion on it. We try to do everything possible to stop the distribution of immoral material.
I am interested in the fact that the minister is going to look over this book and that he is justifying his doing so on the ground that it is in the interests of Canadian morals.
His are incorruptible.

Then, after he reads it he is going to call in somebody else to read it, so that his will not be the only opinion. I

should like to ascertain the degree of exclusion of immoral books or magazines from the mails during the past year. The minister has mentioned that he acts only at the request of the attorneys general of the different provinces.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I would say it is the duty of the attorney general of the province to see to that.

The right to use the mails to transmit money for lottery tickets to another country and to receive tickets from that country has been denied by the Post Office Department. Was that decision made by the Postmaster General in his department, or was it made at the request of the attorneys general of the. several provinces? It is difficult, I realize, for anyone to set up as a censor and determine what is good and what is proper. The minister says he has that power, but apparently he relies on the customs department to bar objectionable books and magazines from entering Canada. Of publications produced in Canada, have any during the past year been barred from the mails?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
No. So far
as lottery tickets are concerned, there is a section in the Post Office Act dealing with them, and it is easy to determine whether it is an illegal lottery. But it is more difficult to say whether a book is immoral.

I brought this matter up yesterday when the amendment to the Canada Evidence Act was going through. It does seem to me that one of the means by which the circulation of these so-called crime comics in Canada might be stopped would be through denying them the use of the mails. I confess I had not actually looked at one of these crime comics until samples were sent to me by the parent-teachers' association of my own city. Under the guise of some slogan such as "Crime does not pay", they appeal to children, who read them and see in every picture the portrayal of some crime of violence or sexual offence, or something of that kind. The attorney general of the province cannot deny the use of the mails to these magazines, but I think the Postmaster General can. If he would look at one of these books I am sure that he would have no hesitation in saying that is contributes to juvenile delinquency and is therefore an offence under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, and that he can use his power to deny such books the use of the mails. The ones I have seen are printed mostly in Toronto. They are not all brought in from the United States. When the embargo

speakerposition: Postmaster General

Many of
these publications go in bundles to the different stores where they are sold. If the Postmaster General had to assume the duties of censor, we should need a lot more employees. Then, in addition, mail matter is secret. We are not supposed to open a sealed envelope. I will look at the publication and refer it to the Minister of Justice, because I doubt my capacity to judge for all the people of Canada. Different people have different standards of what is moral and immoral.
I will send over samples to the Postmaster General. He will see that they are given second-class mail privileges by his department.

I should like to carry this matter a little further. The minister has decided, in the interest of the country as a whole, to read this book on the sex life of the male. After he determines that in his opinion it should be denied the use of the mails, what course will he follow? What has he in mind? Doctor Bates of Toronto drew my attention to the book that has been mentioned.
He is head of the health league.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes, and he asked me to do something about it. I shall have to get the book and look at it or ask somebody to look at it for me.

You should not

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: When I was crown prosecutor I had a storekeeper arrested and we confiscated quite a lot of books he had for sale which in my opinion were immoral. I put in the box a witness who had read these books and he declared them immoral, but much to my surprise two ministers of religion came along the next day and swore that the books were not immoral. I had not read the books myself because I had not time; but the judge, who was a man of sound common sense, said, "I shall read them and decide for myself whether they are immoral". He read them and declared that they were immoral. The books were confiscated and the accused was found guilty.

A good deal has been said with reference to this. When the minister was before the committee with his bonus bill I made some remarks, and I am not going to make any extended remarks at this time, except to say that this discrimination with regard to rural mail contracts still continues. For instance, a month ago I placed on Hansard some of the discriminations with reference to contracts.
Dealing only with the rural mail contracts in my own constituency, I cite the man who has a 16-mile mail route. He gets $1,000, and at the same time the mail courier, driving over a 26-mile mail route, both of them being very much alike, except that the 26-mile route is a little more hilly, receives only $902.50. In other words, he is penalized to the extent of $97.50 for having to drive ten miles further.
I could give parallel cases, but I will mention just one more. In my constituency there is a mail courier who drives a 17-mile route and receives $1,200, while another man not far away, driving a 28-mile route, gets $1,100. In other words, the man who is going the longer distance by thirteen miles is penalized $100 for driving the extra mileage.
That is one thing against the tender system. A few days ago in my own constituency a man who had been driving on a mail contract for fifteen years, having given excellent service, and having received $625, decided that he should get a little more. He took the matter up with the office, urging that he should receive $150 more, but the office called for tenders. When this man saw that there were other people tendering for the contract, he thought he would also put in a tender for $600, seeing that he had the equipment. Somebody else comes in with a tender which is $5 or perhaps $1 less and takes the contract from this man who has given fifteen or sixteen years of service. At the end of another year this man who has tendered at a little less than $600 can get a bonus of $125. This system of tendering is one that should be done away with. I would appeal again to the minister, as I have done before, to have a committee of this house set up to study rural mail problems, so that justice will be done these people. At present they are labouring under an injustice.

There may be nothing in the estimates directly related to that; but on departmental administration, under the estimates of trade and commerce, with the situation as it is in respect of Canadian trade, I should think the committee would expect a statement from the minister on that subject.
