speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I think the facts regarding the European recovery program are well known to hon. members. An appropriation has been made by congress to cover the first fifteen months' requirements. The amount is now being reconsidered. At the moment, I believe, something over $5 billion is the amount of the appropriation for the first fifteen months of the five-year program. Of that, provision is made for off-shore expenditures, perhaps up to an amount of S1,S00 million. According to a press statement made within the last two days, Mr. Bissell, Mr. Hoffman's assistant, stated that, from that fund set aside for off-shore purchases, purchasing from Canada was proceeding very well for the reason that Canadian prices are satisfactory to those administering the European recovery program.
Funds allocated to the United Kingdom are at present being used to pay for wheat and
Supply-Trade and Commerce

meat products and certain other products that are being shipped from Canada. The program provides that trade will flow through the normal channels. It is not the intention of ERP administration that government buying shall be a feature of ERP, unless government buying of the particular commodity was the practice before ERP came into being.
Funds are being allocated to sixteen recipient countries, and anyone wishing to sell goods to those countries under ERP must approach the countries through the usual channels and have his articles included in the requisition from the country concerned.
The Department of Trade and Commerce has obtained the services of Mr. Sidney Pierce who was formerly our ambassador to Mexico, to head up our ERP organization abroad. He has just returned from Washington and will leave within the next few days for Paris, which is the headquarters of the overseas ERP organization.
I have had conversations with those administering ERP; with all senior officials. Mr. Pierce has recently returned from further conferences with them. We both believe that Canada's position in the program is well established. I do not know that there is anything further that I can add. If there are any questions I shall be glad to answer them.

Does the minister mean that the United States has allocated a certain amount of the $5 billion to each of these sixteen receiving countries in Europe and that selling has to be done directly by the supplying countries to those individual recipient countries? Once an order is received by a Canadian supplier, must it be authorized by ERP? Will he explain the procedure? What is the type of products that Canada will be able to supply, not from the standpoint of our ability to produce but from the standpoint of the products being authorized? Will it be raw material products or processed or partly processed products, such as canned goods, that will be sold to the receiving country or to the ERP board?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
This list of availabilities that Canada has submitted to the ERP administration was submitted some two or three months ago. A revised list was submitted within the last few days. I have not that list at hand, but I shall be glad to have it here this evening and give any information from it that the hon. member may wish to have. It must be thoroughly understood that the letter "R" in the ERP program stands for "Recovery" and not "Relief". We must all be careful not to regard ERP as a dumping ground for unwanted

surpluses. That has been made clear by the administration, and I should like to make it clear in this house. The purchases that will be made will be purchases that the recipient countries require for the recovery program. Machinery will be given high priority. Food, of course, is more in the nature of relief than recovery, but is necessary to recovery in some cases. My present information is that all the food that Canada can produce-that is, staple foods such as wheat, which is the most concentrated, high-protein food in existence-will be required. Fish is more a borderline case. I cannot state definitely about that, although it is quite in order for those interested in selling fish to attempt to sell it to the recipient countries. If they can succeed in having it included on the list, there is a fair possibility that it may be approved. But the general situation is that those who have been selling abroad should continue to sell abroad. If they succeed in getting their material on the requisitions from a particular country, then those requisitions will be "vetted" by the ERP administration. If the list is approved, then the material qualifies for sale under ERP.
Does ERP itself place the order?

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. May I continue by saying that, since this is the first time the minister has appeared before
the committee with his estimates for this department, it was surprising to some of us that he did not come prepared to give a fairly comprehensive statement as to the work carried on by this department and as to what is anticipated in the immediate future. However, since the minister has not seen fit to do that, we shall probably have to grope around in the dark and gather up the loose ends, so to speak.
Before I endeavour to make my little contribution, may I assure the minister that I am glad to see that he finds time to take care of this department. I hope he will not take it amiss when I say that when I heard of his appointment as minister in charge of this department, the first thought that struck me was that the minister is much more suited and much better trained to be a builder than to be a trader. However, some of us may be wrong in that respect. It is to be hoped that the energetic leadership that he can give to this department will prove that the fears of myself, and of other hon. members who think as I do, were unwarranted.
I have had an opportunity on several occasions, particularly last summer, to view some of his work; and, now that he is Minister of Trade and Commerce, I hope he will make an effort to see that full use is made of his work in other lines and other years. I have particular reference to the fact that the minister and" his department can be of considerable assistance to those of us who would like to see more trade into and out of Hudson bay, making use of the Hudson bay port and the Hudson bay route. That is the first point of which I should like the minister to make a special note. In the past the minister devoted a great deal of time and energy to the development of that port; I hope he will now help us prove that the Hudson bay route and port are a feasible undertaking. For my part I do not think we should be satisfied with exporting just a few million bushels of wheat by that means this summer. I believe our objective should be at least 25,000,000 bushels.
That is only one small bit of the whole trade picture. This nation is endeavouring to get back to a peacetime footing, but we have found that our old conception of trade has been largely upset. In the first place, we find trade being carried on under entirely different circumstances, on account of the fact that so many commodities are in short supply, with the result that we have a seller's market. So we must adjust ourselves to meet these conditions.
On the other hand, we should also remember that in the final analysis the best market for

Canadians is the home market. We must not overlook the fact that the first demand on the production of this nation should be the provision of a full, rich life for our own people. Let no one think I am saying I do not believe we should go the limit, even to the extent of denying ourselves if necessary, in helping to provide foodstuffs and other commodities for people in lands less fortunate than ours. Nevertheless we should so organize our trade within our own country that our own people will reap the benefit of the wonderful productivity of this country. Here again the minister and his department can give a great deal of leadership.
I hope we shall never again see British Columbia apples going to waste, while at the same time the children on the prairies are not able to obtain apples, and similar conditions in other parts of the country. I hope we may never again see the textile warehouses piled high, and at the same time, as was the case in the not too distant past, the people of this country lacking sufficient and proper clothing. So I say trade should be carried on for the benefit of our own people; then, in branching out into international trade, we should be in a position to trade our surplus goods for commodities we cannot economically produce in our own country, so that our people may be able to round out a full and satisfying life.
In that connection I think it is of considerable significance that at the present time we should have in progress in our own country an international trade fair or exhibition. While the public as a whole are not invited to attend, I believe this fair gives us an idea of what may happen in future. At such a gathering of nations each is able to show the others its commodities, and we can start trading with one another, thus disposing of our surplus products in exchange for commodities we require. I believe in this I am expressing the opinion of hon. members who have had an opportunity' to visit the trade fair and learn at least something of what is going on there.
Then I think I should mention that today our trade is not on the same basis as in. the years gone by. We find that instead of trading being carried on in a haphazard manner, with buyers and sellers running around at loose ends, with people bidding against each other to run prices down or bidding against each other to run prices up, more and more the principal importing countries are buying through import boards or government agencies in order to meet their requirements. So I think we must realize that the old days of laissez-faire are gone, and we

must adjust ourselves to new circumstances and a new order. I would say that Canada is in a very favourable position; and if the Department of Trade and Commerce bears in mind the points I have mentioned I believe it can be of great assistance to the people of this country.
I do not intend to deal with any specific items, Mr. Chairman, though I may do so later on. In conclusion, however, once more I would appeal to the minister to help us make this a banner y'ear for the Hudson bay route.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: As I stated, trade practices are being followed. For example, we have been making bulk sales to the United Kingdom of foodstuffs. The ERP organization has approved those contracts. We shall continue to ship under those contracts to recipients of ERP funds.
Will the payment be made at Washington or London?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: London. The ERP does not buy or sell or pay; it just makes funds available to recipient countries for use in buying articles on an approved list of commodities. The list must be in detail. For example, if a country requires leather, it decides where it wants to buy that leather. The transaction is put up .to the ERP organization, presumably in Paris. If it wishes to buy leather from Canada or from a specific firm in Canada, that is specified. The ERP organization approves or does not approve the transaction. If it is approved, the purchaser will qualify for payment from ERP funds.
How do we specify for United States funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Everything we sell is for United States funds or Canadian funds unless we make some other arrangement.

If the contract were made through London, if we were selling to Great Britain, or through Paris, if we were selling to France, and we were following the normal course of trade we could not insist upon United States dollars. How do we make sure that we get United States dollars on these ERP shipments?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The transaction may be made in sterling. The Bank of Canada has clearing arrangements with the Bank of England. If it is made in convertible currency the transfer can be made. It would have to be a purchase authorized by the Bank of England. If it is authorized, clearance is through the bank. Our sales to the United Kingdom of wheat and food and most other commodities are in Canadian dollars.

It is difficult to understand exactly what does happen. Taking leather, the example the minister gave us, let us say that France needs so much sole leather and will get it in Canada with ERP approval. The Canadian tanner would ship to France against a draft in dollars or United States dollars or francs. That is what would happen when you are trying to maintain ordinary trade channels. I do not quite understand how we get the United States dollars which we are after and which are being provided for this purpose. Would the shipment be segregated from all other shipments going to France, so that we could get United States dollars?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to the Canada Year Book, between 1S67-the date of Con-
Private Bills-Divorce

federation-and 1900, there were less than 20 divorces a year in Canada. Then in 1903 there were 23; in 1909, 51 and, in 1913, 60; less than one per 1,000 marriages.
One of the consequences-and not the least
disastrous at that-of World War I was an increased rate of divorces, due mostly to living conditions in that troubled period, softer laws and easier legal proceedings.
Divorces in Canada numbered 114 in 1918, 608 in 1926, 700 in 1931, 1,570 in 1936 and 2,369 in 1940.
In 1945, last year for which statistics are available, the divorce figures are as follows: Nova Scotia, 158; New Brunswick, 171; Ontario, 1,940; Manitoba, 405; Saskatchewan, 282; Alberta, 575; British Columbia, 1,366; Quebec, 177; Prince Edward Island, 2. This adds up to a total of 5,076 divorces.
In the province of Quebec, where there are no divorce courts, the percentage for 1945 is 3-5 per thousand marriages, compared with 26-9 in British Columbia and 38-2 in Ontario.
In 1947, in the latter province alone, 3,936 divorces, an all-time high, were granted by the supreme court. In 1946, there had been 3,500.
Divorces are increasing at an alarming rate in Canada.
The family, which is the basis of society, is being disintegrated with frightening unconsciousness. Divorce is a sure sign that moral standards are on the down grade, that civilization is on the way to disaster and will inevitably be destroyed.
When people have not enough character, religious conviction, courage, abnegation, honesty, charity and honour to respect the most sacred of all contracts, how can we hope that they will respect the laws to which they are subject and all other contracts by which they are bound?
There are many reasons for divorce, although adultery is the only one mentioned. However, in my opinion one of the principal causes of misunderstanding and separation is marriage between people of different faiths.
Following an investigation in the matter, Bishop Page, of the United States Episcopal Church, found a few years ago that only one per cent of those seeking divorces were of the same faith.
If it is true that we must increase the police force in a country where people have no 
respect for religion, I believe we can also say that where the Christian spirit of a people is low, divorces are bound to increase.
Last year, the Ottawa Journal pointed out that parliamentary jurisdiction in the matter of divorce was little short of scandalous. It doubted very much "if in the whole democratic world, there was a more grotesque parliamentary fact than this."
It is sad, not to say revolting, that people's representatives should sanction and condone by their votes decisions based on sham evidence, obvious perjury and summary proceedings trumped up by experts in the matter.
Marriage being a divinely instituted sacrament, men, be they senators, have no power to put asunder "what God hath joined together."
It is false to claim that the privilege, if you wish to call it that, of seeking divorce is a right, just as it is ludicrous to print on reports of those proceedings that in divorcing Mrs. So-and-so from Mr. So-and-so, parliament is passing an act "for the relief" of Mrs. So-and-so.
In 1886, Mr. Joseph Fremont, LL.D., quondam professor at Laval University, pointed out the danger of this procedure in his survey entitled "Divorce and Separation.":
We are fast heading towards recognition of divorce as the generally accepted rule in the country. . . Besides, is it not recognition of the divorce principle to allow it by means of private bills? The privilege of private bills has served to introduce in society all doctrines and theories later sanctioned by law.
In brief, as stated by Mr. Henri Bourassa in an address, the constitution of 1867 has established divorce, as well as marriage as a principle of national organic law. The federal parliament has maintained or established ordinary divorce jurisdictions in seven provinces and set up a parliamentary divorce court for the whole country. Justice Belleau rightfully said:	"Divorce has been thrust upon us by parliament." Technically since 1867, in current practice since 1888. "Parliament has full authority to break up our homes. Unfortunately it cannot salvage the remains."
Children, those innocent victims, are the ones to suffer; thus do children have to pay the price for their parents' selfishness and mistakes. Driven to the gutter by the judges, they will later appear at the bar of the assize court or within the confines of penitentiaries. The greatness, the future and the very life of the nation are at stake. The country is

Private Bills-Divorce
being deprived of the life blood of generations essential to its growth and expansion. Because its vital forces are being exhausted at the source, the country is impoverished. The plague of divorce' is more dangerous than communisirf and all subversive doctrines combined. To defend and to cultivate the Canadian soil, men and soldiers are needed. Where shall we find them if we destroy the family, the source of life from which new harvests should forever spring?
Let us stem the wave of heathenism that is sweeping over the world, curb the ills bred by divorce and restore the Christian social order. Let parliament, once for all, leave off being a party to these crimes and unruliness and, at long last, decide to disallow every request for divorce brought to its attention. In voting against these bills, I feel that I am doing my duty and contributing to Canada's moral well-being.

Mr. Speaker, may I add a word to support what has been said by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) regarding the bills before us.
I do not intend to make a long speech. In addition to the statistics given us by the hon. member there are two reasons why the thought of divorce is increasingly prevalent among the people. First obscene literature, second, the movies.
Under the Quebec law, children may not enter movie houses until they are sixteen. I am happy to say that I supported' that act of the legislative assembly of Quebec, under the Taschereau administration, as member for the county I now represent in this House of Commons.
Pictures showing a husband philandering with the maid or a wife with her chauffeur, scenes we witness nearly every day in the American films, are bound to corrupt our young people.
The province of Quebec is often criticized because of this act, which is believed to infringe upon the freedom of the individual. However, it does nothing of the sort, but merely curtails the liberty of those who cannot exercise it wisely, that is, of all young people under sixteen years of age.
I therefore subscribe to the hon. member's remarks, and I suggest that authorities do everything in their power to prevent young people in other provinces taking advantage of
those laws which allow youths of all ages to go to the movies. Salacious and obscene literature should be banned more particularly, along with anything that may tend to make our young people consider divorce as a very normal thing and suggest to them the well-known saying: "How can it be so bad, when everybody is doing it?"

Mr. Speaker, I do not see what we can do with these bills except to pass them. This is the ninety-ninth day of the session and we should be getting on with the business of parliament. These bills originate in the other place. The fee over there is $200, and there is a fee of $500 for private bills that come before this house. I repeat, there is nothing that we can do, as far as I can see, but to pass these bills. The government has no policy in relation to them. They are private bills, and the parties affected have paid their fees.
I may say, sir, that I am a member of a church that has made an extensive inquiry into the question of divorce. An important investigation into this question was presided over by the Archbishop of York, and attended by the Right Rev. Bishop Wand of London. They have submitted a report to the Lambeth conference in England, which meets on the first of July for six weeks. The report widens somewhat, for the first time in 300 years, the grounds of divorce. The Church of Scotland is looking into the question of divorce and so are other churches in the old land. The whole question is under consideration by these bodies.
In view of these facts, surely we can pass these bills now, and perhaps next year some method can be proposed in parliament by which the problem of divorce can be handled, so far as legislation here is concerned. I see no purpose to be served by holding up these bills now on this the ninety-ninth day of the session. There is no other course open to us than to pass them.

Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved the second reading of Bill No. 206, to amend the Penitentiary Act, 1939.
He said: There are just three clauses to this bill, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to get the opinion of the responsible minister on it. The first section of the bill provides that a grand jury, members of parliament and others may inspect these institutions. The object of this section is to give jurisdiction to the grand jury and members of parliament to examine into complaints made, and to make presentments without expense to the country. These institutions are managed by the crown, and it is the intention of the bill to afford the people some reliable and definite knowledge of the conditions prevailing in them. The practice recommended here is intended to serve the public interest, and is in no way to be deemed a criticism of the existing system of inspection. On the contrary, the object of the bill is to assist in satisfactory administration. It is a well known fact that these institutions are inspected only by crown officers, and it was one of the cardinal principles of Magna Carta that the people themselves should take a large share in the administration of these penal institutions. Rightly or wrongly, they are now managed by crown officers and no one knows what is going on in them. I believe that in the public interest this situation should not be permitted to continue. Just in passing, let me say that, in the provincial realm, in one of the asylums under provincial authority two sane people were found; and that should not be. There are no visitors to these places.
The second section of the bill gives permission, as has been recommended by some judges, for inmates of these institutions to visit a dying relative. It is felt that this would be a good change. This section is intended to meet cases which occasionally arise when
Penitentiary Act

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
urgent requests are received from relatives of prisoners for permission to visit dying parents or dependents. A recent case of this kind received wide sympathy.
The last section is designed to ascertain what has been happening in regard to real law reform in this country. We are miles behind the old land in this regard. There people are allowed time in which to pay their fines. They have broadened the summary offenders act, and as a result half the prisons in England have been closed. We shall never make any headway in this regard unless all the provinces get together. We are living in an age of conferences, however, and that should be possible. This section deals with offenders under the age of nineteen, who should not be admitted to these institutions. The provinces should provide places for them. If that were done I believe we would have some real law reform.
I should think more hon. members would take an interest in these matters, in view of the money we spend in the upkeep of these institutions. However, it seems we have very little time to devote to this problem, which is one of the most important we have to consider at the present time. If no other hon. members wish to speak, probably the minister will have a word to say.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INSPECTION OF PENAL INSTITUTIONS BY GRAND JURY AND MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I should like to express my appreciation of the interest taken by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Church) in penitentiary matters and in the proper treatment of those convicted of offences. He has made this proposal in the house on other occasions. To some extent the matter was discussed last year, and at that time I started to express the opinions of the Department of Justice, and my own opinions, on the merits of the bill introduced at that time, which is being introduced again this year by the hon. gentleman.
This bill contains three sections, to which I shall have to refer to some extent in what I have to say tonight, though ordinarily one does not refer to particular sections in dealing with a bill on second reading. The first of the three sections of the bill provides for the inspection of penitentiaries by grand juries. Last year I tried to point out that this provision would have very limited application, for the reason that in many of the provinces of Canada there are no grand juries. Indeed there are only two counties in Canada where grand juries would be eligible under the bill to inspect federal institutions. One is the county of Westmorland, New Brunswick, where Dorchester penitentiary is situated; the other is the county of Frontenac, Ontario, where two penitentiaries are located, one at Kingston and one at Collin's Bay. There are no grand [Mr. Church.1
juries in the province of Quebec or in the western provinces, where the other penitentiaries are situated.
There does not seem to be any good reason why this parliament should endow the grand juries of these two counties in Canada with this inspectional function. It must be borne in mind that grand jurors have no particular or special training in inspectional work. They have no particular knowledge of criminology or anything of the kind. For this reason, among others, one of my predecessors in the justice department, Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, opposed a similar bill introduced by my hon. friend in 1930. In my remarks on this bill last year I started to quote what Mr. Lapointe said at that time. I was interrupted because the time devoted to public bills had expired, and I was unable to finish the quotation. I should like to finish it now, because Mr. Lapointe stated why this proposal should not be accepted, in very much better language than I could improvise at the moment. He said:
May I point out that such an inspection of a penitentiary as is proposed by this bill would occupy the activities of a grand jury working ten hours a day for several months? May I also mention the fact that the grand juries are composed of excellent men indeed, but they are men with no especial experience in criminology or the handling of criminals, or the management or care of such institutions. Moreover, grand juries are selected and appointed* by provincial governments and they have therefore no authority whatever in dominion government institutions. Penitentiary officials are not permitted to inspect provincial institutions, nor is it considered desirable that this should be so, notwithstanding the fact that there are confined in mental disease hospitals of the various provinces a number of inmates of penitentiaries, the care and maintenance of whom are paid by the penitentiaries branch. There is already in the penitentiary law all that is required in the matter of inspection. Penitentiaries are inspected in detail by the superintendent, three inspectors, the auditor, the parole officer, the chief penitentiary engineer and the structural engineer. Such inspections are made continuously throughout the year. In addition to that, the following persons are entitled to visit and inspect a penitentiary during business hours: the Governor General of Canada, although I admit that he does not avail himself of that opportunity; the lieutenant-governor of any province of Canada: any member of the king's privy council of Canada, any member of any executive council of any of the provinces, any member of parliament of Canada and any judge of any court of record in Canada or in any of the provinces; and such inspection is invited.
May I say in that regard that the condition and the management of our penitentiaries have been favourably commented upon, indeed have been commended by visitors from other countries connected with various organizations, the judiciary or the police forces, and that our penitentiaries compare favourably with such institutions in any other country in the world?

Penitentiary Act
The citation. I have just read is to be found on page 277 of Hansard of March 4, 1930. Since that time, there have been developments of a beneficial nature in penitentiary administration. Since last year, when the act appointing the commissioner and two deputy commissioners was proclaimed there has been considerable improvement in the penitentiary system, and I think what Mr. Lapointe said in 1930 about the administration and the inspection of a penitentiary would have even more force at the present time. The bill came up later in the session of 1930, and Mr. Lapointe is reported on page 365 of Hansard of March 6, 1930, as follows:
Parliament in the exercise of its powers has established a system of inspection of penitentiaries which is to be found in the sections of the Penitentiary Act that I mentioned' the other night. Some if not all the provinces in the exercise of their powers have authorized grand jurors to inspect provincial prisons. Parliament has done what it considered wise in its field, and the provinces have similarly provided a system which they consider advisable in thedr own field. It would be just as illogical for a province to pass a bill authorizing inspection of provincial institutions by inspectors of penitentiaries as for parliament to adopt this bill. If parliament is of opinion that the present system of inspection which it has authorized is not sufficient or should be improved, its duty is to amend its existing provision so as to provide a better system of inspection under its own direction and control, but from a constitutional point of view it "would be a very bad precedent if parliament were to surrender its control of the inspection of these federal institutions and to entrust that control to a body of men appointed by the provinces for provincial purposes. That is with regard1 to clause 1 of this bill.
I am sorry that I have to take up the bill clause by clause, but it is necessary to do that because it is not possible to sum up the principle of the bill as a whole without referring to the individual sections. Section 2 of the bill reads:
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this act or any other statute or regulation, the Minister of Justice or Solicitor General or a judge of the supreme or county court of a province, in special, urgent and important cases, may, on such terms as are defined in each ease, permit a prisoner, under escort, to pay a brief or temporary visit to a dying parent, wife, child or other near dependent.
The power to grant a temporary ticket of leave in appropriate cases is already within the right of the Solicitor General. It is suggested that the extension of such power to supreme and county court judges who have no facilities for obtaining full knowledge of all the circumstances of the prisoner might result in serious administrative difficulties. The section does not define the conditions under which such permission might be granted or by
whom the expenses involved would be paid. It would be impossible to make penitentiary officers available for such duty without disrupting the normal administration of the institutions. The proposal would also be open to representations as to illness and relationships which would be most difficult to verify. Those objections to the proposal were recognized when the matter was being discussed by Mr. Lapointe on the occasion to which I have referred, and this is what Mr. Lapointe said:
The officers of the penitentiary branch, men who have the experience, who have been in control of penitentiaries for many years, are strongly opposed to any such provision. They submit that it would be a very dangerous procedure to adopt, and one that would undoubtedly be abused if introduced. Exaggerated claims as to the degree of illness of relatives or other near dependents would continually be made and would be used as a means of securing the inmate's return for some other cause. Illness of fake relatives or fake near dependents would be a common occurrence if such a bill should become law. Many foreigners, particularly orientals, I am informed, incarcerated in Canadian penitentiaries, claim so many parents, wives, children or other near dependents that should the bill become operative it would call for a considerable expenditure of money and keep the guards busy delivering them to the homes of parents, wives, children or other near dependents. In one case alone within the past year nine orientals presented themselves at a Canadian penitentiary, all claiming to be close relatives to the one incarcerated.
Mr. Stevens:	They are all cousins.
Mr. Lapointe:	Probably. The necessity for
strict enforcement of the law in all its aspects in connection with the criminal is more apparent today than at any previous time in the history of Canada, because there is an unprecedented increase in the number of convictions for serious crimes and consequently a tremendous increase in prison population. I admit there are some cases which may evoke sympathy, but this provision would lead to such dangers and serious abuses that I do not think it would be desirable to bring about the change suggested. There was a case-and probably it is the one my hon. friend mentioned in his explanatory note-that came to my attention some time ago. The man made and pressed an application for permission of this kind which I could not grant, but what I did was to refer the matter to the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) who is in charge of the administration of the Ticket of Leave Act in order to see whether that convict could not he released under ticket of leave if circumstances would permit his release so that he might visit his parent who was sick. But unfortunately that was a bad ease, one in which it was impossible to grant a release. That man had a very bad criminal record and could not be released under the circumstances and under the practice as it exists. This clause also, I submit, should not be adopted by parliament and the law relating to incarceration should remain as it is.
I have no knowledge of the facts or the circumstances referred to by Mr. Lapointe in
Penitentiary Act

that passage; but the conclusion that he comes to with regard to the general principle of delegating this power of release of convicts under those circumstances to supreme and county court judges is one with which I agree. The position that he took with reference to that proposal was, I believe, a sound one, and I am afraid that I shall be unable to accept the proposals of the hon. gentleman in that regard.
There is still another section of the bill, which reads as follows:
No person under nineteen years of age on his or her last birthday shall be admitted to or be confined in any penitentiary or other penal institution under the control or administration of the parliament of Canada, notwithstanding any law, usage or custom to the contrary and the provisions of any statute applicable to an offender under sixteen years of age shall apply to such person.
The manner in which that was met by Mr. Lapointe when he was minister of justice, was as follows. It may very well be that the conditions which he described are not quite applicable to the present day, but at any rate I am sure that his statement will be of interest to the house. He said this at page 366 of Hansard, of March 6, 1930:
My hon. friend said the other day that he is pleased that we are going to have preferred institutions for young convicts. As a matter of fact, this is now being worked out. The properties have been secured and the building will be erected during the course of the next fiscal year, and when that is done all the young convicts will be segregated and will have no contact with the old, hardened criminals. While this is being worked out, I do not think that this bill should be passed. My hon. friend does not indicate where these young offenders should be placed. If he suggests that they should be sent to the provincial jails. I do not think that there is anything to commend that course. As a matter of fact, evidence has been taken quite recently by the big brother and child welfare representatives as to conditions in the various jails, and it would appear from their report that they certainly would not support such a change. There is not the close supervision in the provincial institutions that exists in the penitentiaries, and there are in the provincial jails old, hardened criminals who have spent their life in jail and who are associating with the juvenile offenders with a good deal less supervision than in the penitentiaries to prevent them from placing their imprint upon all those with whom they come in contact. These old criminals have more opportunities in the jails than they have in the penitentiaries to exert an evil influence on the young delinquents. This change, therefore, would certainly not be desirable while the new system of preferred institutions is being erected.
There was some further discussion of this particular provision, all of which will be found in the report of the debate in Hansard of March 6, 1930, and the debate was adjourned,
I believe, after this discussion took place.

The report that I have from the officers of the penitentiaries on this proposal of my hon. friend is not favourable to its adoption. The objection taken by them is that the section, indeed the bill, does not state what disposition is to be made of persons under the age mentioned, that is the age of nineteen, who have been convicted of serious crime and have been sentenced to two years or more. The bill also proposes that the provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act shall apply to such persons. The suggestion of the penitentiary officials is that it is better to leave to the discretion of the sentencing judge or magistrate the decision as to where the youthful offender should be sent, since the facilities available for their incarceration vary in the different provinces.
I think that is probably all I should say with regard to the bill before the house. It serves the useful purpose of bringing forward the whole question of penal reform, in which there is a very great interest in this country, and when the penitentiary estimates are reached I shall be expected1, of course, to say something about what has been done during the past year and what our plans are with regard to the future. It would appear that the particular objectives sought to be attained by the enactment of this bill are likely to be better attained in another way, by the adoption of other machinery.

I wish to refer to these estimates and to point out certain matters in connection with the Department of Trade and Commerce. I would invite the attention of hon. members to the international trade exhibition which is now in progress at the exhibition grounds in the city
of Toronto. That exhibition will give them a very good idea of what has been accomplished in the past, and what under proper policies can still be achieved in the future by the Department of Trade and Commerce, for the promotion of the trade of this dominion, the fifth trading nation of the world. Hon. members have only to visit that exhibition to see the results of the old policies in connection with trade and commerce which we had in Canada before the new ideas were put into effect. These new trade ideas that we have today do not work for the benefit of Canada.
As I have said, the department whose estimates are now before the committee is one of the most important in the Canadian public service, but its possibilities do not seem to be fully recognized. We are sending ambassadors and consuls general and other dignitaries of that kind all over the seven seas, but they do not accomplish what the trained officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce can. There is no department that means more to the Canadian businessman than this department, which has been efficiently operated, as the trade exhibition shows. When we turn to Geneva, however, and examine all the pacts which are now written into the estimates at pages 68 and 69, exports and imports, we find that the whole situation has been changed, so much so that the Canadian businessman does not know where he stands, with all the forms that have to be filled out.
This department has done splendid work, and its representatives throughout the world are the men who bring business to this country and who build up Canada from coast to coast. They find trade for us. They find outlets for our products of sea, soil, forest and mine, and altogether they have done a magnificent job in the past.
I hope that you, Mr. Chairman, and other members as well will go and see that trade exhibition. There are within the sterling area many countries that can contribute to the building up of Canadian trade, and the fact is that in the past we have always depended upon the sterling area and the mother country in particular. She has been a steady customer for all our farm products, wheat, grain and flour, and for manufactured goods of all kinds. We have had a steady market there and she has undoubtedly been our best customer. It is not

a market that is here today and gone tomorrow. Unfortunately, however, it has been largely interfered with by what has been done at Geneva.
