When the government comes to a stock-taking in the next trvelve months it will find what the present policies have meant to this country. The government has by Geneva, turned down our best customers. One of the ministers has gone to Ontario, and he predicts that the government will throw overboard the finest customer we have ever had for our cattle overseas, and allow our cattle to go to the United States. The district represented by the hon. members for Davenport, Spadina, Trinity and Parkdale, and all the area north of Queen street, were built up by the great agricultural industry of Massey's and the cattle business to Britain as well. But now, as I say, our best customer has been thrown overboard.
Let hon. members visit the exhibition to which I have referred and they will see with their own eyes what the sterling area has meant in the past to this country, and can compare the results of the past with what we are likely to have in the years to come.
I am a firm believer in the old two-party system. One of my hon. friends the other day was referring to the song "Hail, hail, the gang's all here", but there was no reply as to his Yale cry from the government. I can say that in my experience I have found that west of the great lakes-I have visited that part of the dominion two or three times-the best policy has been found to be this: Depend upon your best customer always. Further, I would suggest that west of the great lakes our two old parties should end the union governments in Manitoba and in British Columbia and return to the old two-party system, Conservatives and Liberals, because, if they do not, the only alternative is to elect my hon. friends to the left, the C.C.F., as Yale showed the other day. The two old parties have served this country well, and governments under both parties have conducted a Department of Trade and Commerce that has been a credit to the Dominion of Canada. Trade has advanced by leaps and bounds. When you compare the value of this department to the country with that of some of the other departments in which there is duplication such as the Department of External Affairs and others, it will be found that the work is being done by this department which gets the cream of the business and

means something to the trade and commerce of the country. What I think we want in this House of Commons is more of the politics of principle and progress and less of the politics of peanuts and party. I believe that motto could be applied to many departments, especially the Department of Trade and Commerce, when we find that, after the progress and success this country has had, we are to toss it to the four winds of heaven and introduce a new trade system.
I shall now go on to refer to some other matters. The first is the bureau of statistics. I should like to see this department now expand. Let us have some proper survey made of the accidents that happen. Today you cannot tell how many people have been killed on the highways. The situation is better with regard to level crossings, but you cannot tell the loss by fire. I would point to the large number of fires occurring in Ontario, and to the fact that you cannot tell what has been the loss of lives in houses that are burnt down. There is no way of telling that. I hope the bureau of statistics will bring that matter of deaths and those injured for all Canada up to date, and get us an up-to-date report, so that every year we shall have a statement along that line. They have done a great deal of good work in this connection. The returns are not made to them by the provinces, but I think the bureau might expand the work to the extent I have suggested.
In connection with the Canada Grain Act, I am sorry to see what is going on in the department and in the country. We have tossed aw'.ay our best, customer. Our markets were overseas and not north and south. It is an east and west industry and always has been. The markets have always been the markets of the world, Britain, France and her allies. That was a steady market and it has been thrown overboard.
In connection with the tourist business. I may say this is a presidential year, and I doubt if we shall have fulfilled the rosy picture in this travel bureau which is forecast. I venture to say that if we had every year an exhibition such as the one I referred to a moment ago, we might get some trade. But with provincial elections on, the high cost of living, the cost of travel and the lack of hotels, apart from one or two of the big conventions I fail to see where we are to get all these millions of dollars in tourist trade we hope for during this year.
Another matter I should like to refer to is the standards division, administration, and electricity and gas inspection services. I think the time has come when that should be done

Supply-Trade and Commerce
voluntarily by the government. At the present time we need a national policy for cheap light and power. Canada has a potential of forty-six million horsepower, of which only one-sixth or one-seventh is developed at the present time. Some of it is only seasonal. I believe that what we need at the present time is some national policy or measure to deal with the situation in the maritimes, the Northwest Territories, and all Canada. We need a vast national policy with regard to cheap light and power. I was surprised the last time I was in British Columbia some years ago, to find that the richest province of all in water power did not have a cheap light and power program. I believe the government would be well advised to carry out this electricity and gas inspection itself and charge it up to some other branch of the department.
I do not know that I can say anything further. I compliment the minister who is a hard-working one. His predecessor was also a most excellent minister. The trade exhibition of both ministers is one of the finest things I think this country has ever seen. I wish the minister every success in his work, but I am fearful of what will happen in the days that are to come when today we toss, via Geneva, our trade policies overboard and lose our best customers.

The minister a short time ago gave us a glimpse of what was called his program of availability. He did not table the whole schedule of figures, but it is a strange thing that although we do not get those things in the House of Commons, the press seems to get them. I have in my hand here a clipping of May 14 last which reads as follows:
The Washington blueprint is contemplating an expenditure of approximately one billion dollars in Canada by the participating countries, but in the fifty-three categories are some items where Canada's share has been placed .actually above estimated capacity to produce and others in which this country has been left out entirely or cut in on quantities less than she might have expected.
I do not pretend to hold the minister to those figures or to those fifty-three categories that are mentioned there. But as this has found its way into the press, I think the minister ought to tell us something more about the amount of money that is likely to be used with respect to this program. I should like to read just for a moment from the speech which the Minister of Finance made on November 17 last in which he said:
The United States government has now recommended to congress that it should authorize the use of funds voted for aid to Europe in making purchases outside the United States. In the expectation that this policy will be implemented,
we are ascertaining what supplies can be made available from Canada for this purpose. A program of this bind would resemble in many respects the Hyde Park agreement that proved to be so effective and constructive during the war.
As a matter of fact, in my district of Park-dale, apparently representatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce are calling on industry and are saying, "What have you available? What can you do?" I shall not mention the name of the officer, but I am reading from a letter which I should be glad to show the minister. One paragraph reads as follows:
We had a recent visit from Mr. Blank-
I will not give his name.

of the Department of Trade and Commerce who inquired as to our production capacity providing Canada gets orders from the ERP. We appreciated his interest in getting a share of this business for us.
I think the minister ought to take us into his confidence, since this is a Canadian plan -this is our share in ERP-so that we might know what is being done by the Department of Trade and Commerce in this regard and what we may expect. A good number of the commodities in the list which the minister spoke about were in the category of food. On reading excerpts from the speech the minister made in Montreal on May 11 last, I find he made it clear that Canadian industry and Canadian producers were to have to suffer certain sacrifices. I should like the minister to tell us, if he would, what those sacrifices are to be. He is reported as follows:
The Reconstruction Minister said', however, that the recovery program for Europe meant that Canada would be able to carry on export trade at about the same volume as before, avoid a "radical reorientation of industry, and maintain higher levels of investment and income than would otherwise be possible."
He mentioned that there were to be sacrifices by the producers and the consumers in this country before the benefits of the plan would be felt. I gather that in respect to manufactured goods we were to lose some of our markets, and that it would not be possible for us to keep those markets which we had built up over the last three years by reason of what they called our own little Marshall plan of credits. That seems to be perfectly so.
As we know, Canada and Newfoundland are the only two members of the British commonwealth who do not belong to the sterling area; and by reason of that fact we find it difficult to sell our goods in the sterling area. I know the minister has before him particulars showing how our trade with the sterling area is falling down at the present time, and how we are losing those markets. For instance, my
Supply-Trade and Commerce

information is that, because of a world shortage of United States dollars, many currencies are no longer convertible, and a European balance of payments with the western hemisphere is unobtainable. The consequent threat to Canadian prosperity shows ominously in the decline of British imports from this hemisphere from 49 per cent in 1946 to a prospective 34 per cent this year. This figure was 31 per cent in 1938.
I know the minister has received representations from manufacturing concerns and exporters in Canada who have shown that their exports to sterling area countries have fallen off 90 per cent, 95 per cent and in some cases 100 per cent. These industries are asking the minister and his department to carry out the fullest possible investigation in respect of all possible reciprocal trading arrangements with the sterling area countries. Surplus goods are waiting in Canada to be moved to the sterling area, and it is a question of setting up the machinery for the exchange of such goods.
In that respect, and having regard also to the Marshall plan, this afternoon I believe the minister told us that Mr. Pierce, the Canadian representative, was in Paris. We would like to know what sort of blueprint Mr. Pierce has with respect to the movement of these goods and commodities from Canada to Europe. After all, we know the Department of Trade and Commerce considers the United Kingdom and western Europe our natural market. For the time being we have lost that market, and it is necessary that something be done to restore it. Having regard to the fact that we are dependent upon the minister and his department to lead us in this-
Paper chase.

Yes, this paper chase, if you choose to call it that. Certainly when you make sacrifices you want to know what they are. So I should like the minister to explain the plan of which the Minister of Finance spoke in such glowing terms on March 17 last. I have some other questions I should like to ask, but for the moment I think I shall stop there. When we first heard about ERP it was the bonanza that would solve our export problems. Then we heard that it would enable us to hold our own, and that we would be lucky if we got what we did in 1947. Now we are told that it will be a case of making sacrifices. We can make the sacrifices; but industry, the exporters and the general public would like to know what those sacrifices are. I believe the minister is in a position to tell us.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I am very much interested to hear that we have lost all our trade with the sterling countries. I have before me the figures

of our exports to the United Kingdom for the first three months of this year as compared with the first three months of last year. In January, 1947, we shipped $50,500,000 worth of goods. In January, 1948, we shipped $64,900,000 worth. In February, 1947, we shipped $44,900,000 worth of goods; in February of this year, $51,700,000 worth. In March, 1947, we shipped $47,600,000 worth of goods, in March, 1948, $59,200,000 worth. Or if my hon. friend would like a comparison as between the shipments for the first three months of this year and the shipments pre-war I can tell him that the average exports from Canada to the United Kingdom in the years 1935 to 1939 for the month of January were $25,500,000. This year they -were $64,900,000, or two and a half times as great.
But, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Let me get this on Hansard; you brought up the subject. For February the average from 1935 to 1939 was $23,600,000; for February of 1948, it was $51,700,000. The average during those years for March was $26,-
400,000,	as against $59,200,000 this year. For anyone to rise in his place and say our trade with the sterling countries is gone, is just ridiculous.
I did not say that. I said we were losing our trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There is no evidence of that.

I will correct myself in this respect. I was not talking about the United Kingdom alone. I was talking about the other nations in the sterling area as well. The figures that have been given me-and they must be in the hands of the minister and his department-indicate that the sterling area countries have had to put on import controls, as we know; and since Great Britain is the banker for the sterling area countries, they are restricting trade with other parts of the world, including Canada, so that little by little our trade with those countries other than the United Kingdom is dropping. If I am wrong in that the minister may correct me, but those who prepared these figures think otherwise. I believe representations have been made or are to be made to the minister to the effect that these people wish him to do something in that regard; otherwise trade with these dependencies and dominions which form part of the British empire will drop to a point where it will not be funny for Canadian business.

Might I ask the minister if it is not correct that the figures he gave for January, February and March of this year include considerable purchases by the United

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Kingdom under Canadian export credits which it is government policy not to extend from now on?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Included are credits of
$15,000,000 a month, or $45,000,000 in all, which is not a large sum in proportion. The point is that our exports are not dropping. The credits ended in the middle of April, but since that time there has been no reduction in exports.
Why not separate it and tell us what it is?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Separate what from what?

You have so many millions, and you have credits of
S15,000,000 a month; then you have this great increase. What did it? What did we sell that we did not sell before, or what did we sell more of than we sold before? The thing is simple; you have all your information there.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: In these three months we sold goods to the value of $175-8 million, of which $45,000,000 was credits. The rest was paid for.
What were the goods? Where is the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: You want the list?
No, just roughly. Let us quit fooling about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The largest items are foodstuffs. The biggest, is wheat; the next is meat; the next is cheese, and the next is eggs.
The Minister of Agriculture told us he put- on the pressure to get England to take these things, and that is what you are talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Nevertheless we are not talking about how we sold it, but about what we sold.
Then your figures do not mean anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Then there is lumber, and aluminum and other ibase metals, a large item; agricultural machinery, which is a very large item, and various special types of maehineiy.

I should like to ask another question, which follows the first question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. We are told that under ERP the United States will spend 5-3 billion in the first fifteen months of the operation of the plan. Here is the simple figure that I want. What proportion, irrespective of whether it is ERP dollars or any other kind-they are
United! States dollars that are going to buy- will we get in United States dollars, irrespective of source?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I think it would be most difficult to say what portion of the $5,300 million; I am sure I cannot say.
Cannot the minister give us some rough idea of what we shall gain in. United States dollars in the fifteen months' operation of the Marshall plan? That is all I want to know.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The hon. member means how much better off we shall be in United States dollars than we were when we started?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Regardless of whether it is the Marshall plan or anything else?
No, under the Marshall plan. I would like to segregate it. The Minister of Finance does the guessing on the rest of it with his three-pronged fork.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can answer my hon. friend's question if he would like an answer.
I would love it. It would be the first straight answer I have got from the Minister of Finance for quite a while.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only effect which I presume the so-called Marshall plan will have on Canada is that it will help our customers to pay for some of the things they want to buy from us. We have no means of knowing how much of the purchases they make for us is paid for out of Marshall plan dollars.
Why have you not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because they are not paying by dollars.
You said you could answer me if I wanted an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have given an answer.

I know that last Monday was Monday and that next Saturday will be Saturday; to say that would answer me as well as you have, because you did not even address yourself to my question. Surely you must have some idea. We heard from you how this Marshall plan was being looked forward to, to help our United States dollar situation. Now- we have the Marshall plan; we have $5,300 million which is to be spent in fifteen months. You anticipated something if they passed it. We have it now. What was it you anticipated?
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Perhaps I can answer it. My hon. friend somehow has the impression-
Are there any more of you who would like to join in this picture? I was taken away from the minister by the Minister of Finance and I am glad to be back again on your tender mercies.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Some hon. gentlemen opposite have the idea that the Marshall plan is for the relief of Canada. The Marshall plan was designed for the rehabilitation of Europe.
Let us admit that neither one of us is that dumb.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: You are asking what we are to get out of the Marshall plan.
What we shall receive for the goods we sell. Does that make it plain to you?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
No. We sell goods to Europe and we get paid for them in dollars; we sell goods to France and we get paid for them in dollars; we sell goods to Italy and we get paid for them in dollars. The presumption is that if those countries had no ERP aid we would not sell as many goods that we would get paid for in United States dollars. Perhaps my hon. friends can relate that to ERP dollars, but my department has no information as to what proportion of what we sell to those countries will be paid for in ERP dollars.
When one stops to reason that England gets so many ERP dollars to spend anywhere she likes, in Canada, in the United States or in any other dollar country, he can appreciate my difficulty in telling my hon. friend how many ERP dollars will be among the dollars Britain pays to Canada.
There would be an excess over what we are getting now. We know how much gold England has-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, we do not.

-and we know how much gold other countries have. The Marshall plan will help us in our United States dollar position. I agree with you that it is nothing but rehabilitation, but we are perhaps selfish about the matter and will benefit by it in our United States dollar picture. What is the benefit we shall receive? You said you would answer and the Minister of Finance took his crack at the pussy and told me nothing. I would be delighted if the minister would help me and give me some idea. In those fifteen months will it be S200 million, $300 million or what? To me it is a matter of simple arithmetic. Consider that

these various countries will be buying; you know this is new money, new United States dollars which will help those countries to the extent of $5,300 million; by whatever route you take, how much of that will get back to this country in those fifteen months? Perhaps it cannot be answered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course it cannot.

It certainly has not been as yet. The Minister of Finance shakes his head and says it cannot be answered. Perhaps it needs a shake of the head by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to make it unanimous.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The supporting of the United States dollar situation and balances of payment are, course, my particular concern. Perhaps I shall not be stating the obvious if I give my hon. friend some indication of how these balances of payment are met. Hon. members appreciate that countries have to settle their balances with us. In the case of the United Kingdom, they maintain balances with the Bank of Canada. Those balances are credited with the proceeds of the sales of British goods and services in this country. They are credited with transfers which are made by the British government from sources that are unknown to us. Insettlement of those balances, a cheque is in effect drawn on their balance with the Bank of Canada.
Canada has no means of knowing what ERP dollars, if any, that the British receive are transferred to Canada, but we do know as a general rule that if the United Kingdom or any other European country is furnished with a loan or if they receive United States dollars in some other form they will be available for the import of Canadian goods. It is not within our control to determine what dollars are used for what purpose. We know, speaking generally, that if they receive United States dollars they will be available to pay their bills with, but that is all we do know. Nobody can give my hon. friend any more information.

We know this simple thing, that $5,300 million extra United States dollars are to be spent-mark that word "extra"-to help in the rehabilitation of the devastated countries of Europe. We know that, so we can go that far together.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We read that in the newspapers.

That extra money, those extra United States dollars, will come back related in some way to

Supply-Trade and Commerce
purchases made in this country, purchases of goods which the ERP will supply to those devastated countries. If you say "yes" to this,
I am through. Is it the minister's statement, knowing those simple facts, that he has no idea of what proportion of that extra money, that new money, will come to the Dominion of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have none whatever; my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, may have, but I have none whatever.

How do these off-shore purchases work? Is a billion and a half of this $5,300 million handed to the European countries in cash, and then are they told that they can spend that for what and where they please, apart from purchases in the United States? Is that true?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No. Certain allocations of dollars are made to certain countries. Those dollars are earmarked for special uses. The recipient country submits a list of purchases that it would like to make, what it would like to buy and where it would like to buy it. Those lists are either approved or not approved by the ERP administration. If they are approved and if on a list there are dollars earmarked for purchases in Canada, those purchases qualify for ERP funds and can be charged against ERP funds allocated to that country.
Are those lists prepared and approved now, or are they still in the formative stage?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: They are prepared from time to time. I understand that a quarter of a year is the unit for which lists are submitted. The lists are being made up now for the second quarter and are being studied. No doubt in due course they will be approved, after which purchases will be made.

Will the minister try to tell us as much as he can about this, instead of having us go at it by these prying questions? For instance, I think the Minister of Finance said there was no way of knowing how much money would come to Canada, and yet in his Montreal speech the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
In short, we will 'be enabled, through the funds under the Economic Cooperation Act, to carry on our export trade in roughly the same volume and nature as before-avoiding a radical reorientation of our productive system

 and to maintain higher levels of investment and income than would otherwise be possible.
When the minister makes that statement in a public speech I take it that he had something to go on. I may be able to help him. We financed $499 million of our export trade 5849-306
last year by Canadian export credits. That was the figure given in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance. May we understand that approximately that sum, $500 million, will be available from this source, and if it is not available from this source, from what other source of United States dollars will it be available? How much has already been spent under ERP requisitions in Canada? I submit to the minister that if he would tell us all he can we would get along much faster and I think we would be all greatly benefited by the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am sorry but I can only give the amount of exports from this country. We have lent this year about $52,500,000. Everything else has been paid for in dollars. I cannot tell the hon. member about ERP dollars, because I do not know and the Minister of Finance does not know, and I doubt whether anybody in Ottawa knows. I assure my hon. friend that the answer is not obtainable.
I would have thought it was the duty of the minister to make a forecast.

I thought I did not know anything about ERP, and I listened hoping to find out something; but, after listening to this debate, I am satisfied that I know as much about it as anybody else.
I think the Department of Trade and Commerce never gets the credit that is coming to it. I have travelled quite a bit in my life and in any city you visit abroad you will find a representative of the trade and commerce department. We can send any old defeated politician to be an ambassador, but you cannot send anybody who does not know his business to represent the trade and commerce of this country. I have had an opportunity of attending meetings of the united nations in three successive years, and I found that even our external affairs people needed the representatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce to guide them before they could make agreements. The importance of this department is not sufficiently recognized. Looking over these estimates, you find that they are mainly for salaries for people who are rendering service to the different communities in which they reside and to the trade of this dominion.
I have one complaint. Our goods are not ' advertised enough in other countries. I was over in the old country in 1938 and 1945. We can send lots of Nova Scotia and British Columbia apples to Great Britain, and they are well liked there but they are not sufficiently advertised. We must do some good
Supply-Trade and Commerce

advertising. I took up with the previous minister of trade and commerce the question of advertising our bacon, but I found that that cannot be done under the regulations. But just as soon as possible I hope that the department will put on a real advertising campaign in other countries. Everybody would benefit from it from the top right down to the bottom, or from the bottom right up to the top, whichever way you like to take it.
What about the middle?

You pass that going up or down.
I support what the hon. member for Humboldt said and urge that the minister help to make our Manitoba seaport at Churchill boom this fall. With modern equipment we shall be able to have a longer season there. I have been in touch with captains who sail that route and they say it is much easier coming in by the Hudson bay route than coming up the St. Lawrence river, because you can set your ship on three or four courses to the port of Churchill, whereas you have to change your course several times coming up the St. Lawrence river.
Might I, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, say something about grain? Would the minister make an announcement about what is coming to the farmers? I think it was a mistake on the part of the government to throw grain on the open market on October 22 of last year. I have received many letters from farmers wanting to know what adjustment they will get, and I have also grain companies wanting to know what will happen to them. The small grain companies which buy in small quantities, just a few carloads or a few thousand bushels, which they have to turn over immediately, will never be able to pay what the large companies can, which have huge elevators and huge storage facilities. These larger companies will be able to pay a much greater return to the farmer than the little company, with less capital, which has to have a quick turnover.
What about the wheat pools?
They are the big companies; they will pay, and some of the other grain companies will pay.
They have not paid yet.
I do not think any of them have paid yet.

Several independent
companies have paid.
You make your speech when the time comes.
We just wanted to help you.

You are not helping me, or you would not be sitting there. I would ask the minister to make a statement and tell us what the policy of the government is with respect to this matter. I think you fellows made an awful mistake when you threw the grain on the open market. The people did not want that.
They know that now.

Yes. Prosperity goes to a man's head and he forgets conditions in the 1930's. The farmer will never have prosperity until he has stable prices for his products, based on the cost of production and taking into consideration the prices he has to pay for what he has to buy. I hope the minister will make an announcement, so that I can reply to the people in the constituency of Selkirk and the grain companies that are writing to me to know what the government intends to do in the matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I still think it would be wise for the committee to stick to the item before us. Item 458 has to do with the Canada Grain Act, and so forth. If we were discussing that item the minister would have the proper officials before him.
I asked your permission before I started, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I still think we would make more progress if we deal with the items as we come to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
My hon. friend was very courteous in asking his question; and, since he said nice things about the department, I think I should answer his question regarding the port of Churchill. I saw Mr. Dalgleish, one of the operators of the line of steamers which has been serving that port since the elevator was built. He told me that he had more inbound freight for Canada this year than ever before. I spoke to the board1 of grain commissioners. They are filling the elevators there. The principal question will be the lateness of the crop. This year's crop promises to be a late one. As my hon. friend knows, we have practically no carryover; we have no store of wheat to move to the port until the new crop of wheat arrives. Therefore it may be a poor year in

Supply-Trade and Commerce
wheat, simply because there is no wheat to ship; but we do expect a good year of inbound cargo.
Is the elevator empty now?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is being filled now. The grain is moving to Churchill. The elevator was emptied. I think the elevator was filled at the opening, but I am not sure of that.
It may be filled, waiting for ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes; grain is moving in there now.
It has never been filled in its history.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
Filled?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Certainly, filled almost every winter.
As far as the payments on coarse grains are concerned, we have been waiting for the private grain firms to settle. Some of them have settled. I believe the pools have not settled, and some private firms - have not settled. We feel that for the government to do anything before the private settlements are made would be to disturb the situation, but we do hope that something can be done shortly.
Is there any prospect of a pooling system, so that everybody will be paid alike?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No, that is quite impossible. If there is a payment, it will be a flat over-all payment.	.
It would be the fairest way.

Before this item passes, I should like to support some of the requests made by the hon. member for Humboldt and by the hon. member for Selkirk, and made earlier in the session by the hon. member for Churchill, and by other hon. members, regarding the greater use of the port of Churchill. I make special reference to the utilization of the port in transporting grain at a cheap rate to the maritime provinces. That suggestion has been put forward at different times. The Minister of Agriculture has approved it, and I believe the hon member for Davenport has as well. It is requested that the grain should be shipped from the west through the port of Churchill and Hudson bay by water in order that we in the maritime provinces may obtain feed grains that we have required for so many years, at a cheaper rate because of cheap water transportation. Grain elevators should be built at points in the 5849-306J
maritime provinces such as Pugwash, which has a splendid port; in Prince Edward Island, on the south shore of Nova Scotia and on the bay of Fundy, also on the New Brunswick side, in order that the people of the maritimes might get the benefit of necessary cheap feed grain. I hope that, under the marshland project which has been approved, and which will take some years to become fully effective, we shall be able to produce a larger proportion of feed grains than we have ever done before. Over a long period of years it has been necessary to transport feed grains to our provinces from the west. The Minister of Agriculture has definitely approved the use of the port of Churchill and the Hudson bay route, in order that grain might be transported to the maritime provinces.
I have never been enthusiastic about the soundness of the large expenditures which have been made in building the Hudson bay railroad and developing the Hudson bay port, but perhaps I am not the one to judge. However, expenditures of $50,000,000, $80,000,000 or
S100,000,000 have been made. The results of those expenditures are there for the benefit of all Canada. Hon. members of the committee will agree that the people of the maritime provinces are as much entitled to the benefit of the use of this port as any other part of Canada, if not more so. It has been said in this house many times past in my hearing that grain has been exported from Canada by the cheap water export rate to European countries, and could be brought back to Nova Scotia cheaper than the freight rates on grains sent directly into the maritime provinces from the west. During the last few years we have had the benefit of a subsidized freight rate. We are very grateful for that, but I should like to ask the minister to give special attention to the practicability and desirability of using this route and these facilities to which I have referred, and to build elevators for storage, so that users of feed grain in the maritime provinces may get advantage of these facilities.

What are the conditions that a nation has to meet in, order to get aid under ERP? I ask that question, because statements have appeared in the press from time to time that certain limitations have been placed upon the industrial output of some of the nations getting help. For instance, it was said that certain limitations have been placed upon the shipbuilding industries of England, and similar statements have been made about other nations. If that is true, of course it would have a direct bearing upon our trade

Supply-Trade and Commerce
with these nations. I should like to know whether or not the minister has that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The countries receiving ERP assistance are the countries of Europe outside the iron curtain. I can assure my hon. friend that the purpose of ERP is to stimulate production. I would be shocked to learn that any limitation on production is imposed by the program.

I should like to bring to the attention of the committee some facts in connection with asbestos, and to ask the minister some questions concerning the matter. There are two companies, one in Calgary and the other in Vancouver, engaged in the manufacture of building materials from asbestos and cement. These companies make fireproof wall board, shingles, siding, corrugated roofing, coloured tile, sheathing, pipe, eaves-troughing, and a considerable number of other building materials, using as the chief material asbestos fibre and cement. The difficulty at the present time is that these companies cannot get the supply of asbestos fibre. They are depending for that on the two large asbestos producing companies in Canada. As I understand the situation, these companies have never actually refused to ship asbestos and so forth to these two companies. They just put them off, with the result that these building construction materials plants are forced to run very much below capacity, and at times to close down altogether. That is the situation of those companies manufacturing building materials which are in such short supply, which supply the minister has informed the house on numerous occasions he is trying to increase. The fact these companies cannot get the asbestos fibre which they need seems to me absolutely inexplicable.
I have here a copy of a publication put out by authority of the minister-in fact, one has to pay ten cents for it-which gives the figures in regard to asbestos production and exports from the country, and in 1947 production was 661,815 tons, and exports, 636,000 odd tons. In any event, exports were 96-24 per cent. These exports were made up of crude asbestos, 953 tons only; milled fibres-and it is milled fibres which these companies making these building materials require-223,693 tons; waste and refuse, shorts and so forth, of which they can use some 412,000 tons.
In spite of the fact that Canada is a very large producer of asbestos, the way the thing is running at the present time 96% per cent of all asbestos produced is shipped out of the country; and our own plants, particularly in western Canada, where we need building ma-

terials badly, and where we need industries, are unable to get a sufficient supply to maintain production.
The situation is the more peculiar, I think, in the fact that these large asbestos producers ship this material to a large extent to the United States. It is there manufacured into the very building materials these two companies make, and these materials are shipped back to Canada and sold with a consequent considerable loss of United States exchange, wdiich we are trying so hard to conserve at the present time.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the situation as far as these two companies are concerned, and as far, also, as the general running of the asbestos business goes. I understand, further, that the companies to which this asbestos is shipped, where it is made into wallboard, are affiliates or subsidiaries of big producing companies in Canada. Furthermore, at least one of these companies is now7 in the process of building a plant of its own in Montreal to make these building materials, and these two small companies in the west are a little suspicious that they are being denied a supply of asbestos so that they will not build up too big a business and be too hard to compete with when the time comes for the big companies to get their own plant in operation in Montreal. That is as it may be; I do not know. At any rate, this situation exists and it could be cured; it could be eased very readily, I believe, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I have been writing to the minister on the matter for the last two months. On April 12 I w7rote him a letter pointing out how he could readily cure the situation, but nothing has been done about it, I have had a considerable number of letters which have produced no results. They have not got me anywhere, and it is for that reason that I raise the matter now.
This situation could be prevented, and these companies could be assured of a sufficient supply of asbestos fibre to meet requirements, simply by the minister writing a letter to the companies concerned. That would cure the whole situation-just a simple letter. Apart from that, if it did not produce results, all that would be necessary would be to refuse these companies export permits. Everything that is exported from the country at the present time requires an export permit; and if these different asbestos producers will not supply our own local companies with the asbestos they need, which is a very small amount-it would not amount to one-half or one-quarter of one per cent of what is shipped out of the country-if they are not willing, on the basis of a request from the minister,

Supply-Trade and Commerce
to supply these companies, then I am quite sure the thing could be fixed up simply by refusing them an export permit, so that the small amount of asbestos could be supplied to our Canadian users first.
The situation that exists is absolutely ridiculous. I cannot comprehend how it has continued, and I would ask the minister to explain to me why nothing has been done to correct it. I also ask him to take steps along the lines I have suggested, or otherwise to ensure that these companies making building supplies get a sufficient supply of asbestos fibre to keep them going.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I cannot imagine what branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce would be expected to intervene in the case mentioned. My hon. friend is, I assume, an advocate of free enterprise. Why, therefore, he wants the government to step in and control asbestos for the benefit of a plant in Calgary, which surely is able to trade with another private enterprise firm, is beyond my comprehension. He is quite mistaken when he says that export permits are required for asbestos. Products in ample supply are not subject to export control and never have been. Only materials in short supply are subject to such control.
My hon. friend says that the asbestos plants in Canada have associated plants in the United States. That is not true in the case of the largest producer of asbestos and, as far as I know, that company is willing to sell to any purchaser who is willing to pay the current price of the product. I suggest that my hon. friend may explain to his friends that, since they are operating in a free enterprise country, business should be able to look after itself.

I have one or two simple answers to that. This is a supposedly free enterprise country; but under the present government it is far from free in enterprise, for practically everything in the country is controlled. I am not asking the minister to control this thing. All I ask is that he write a letter. I think that would be enough-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend has a stenographer and a pen. Why does he not write a letter?

It is no good my writing a letter. I have no control over the trade and industry of the country as the minister has, and a word from me means nothing. A word from him would mean a lot to these people. He knows that as well as I do. All I ask is that, first of all, he write a letter requesting them to supply these firms in the west. I am quite sure that is all that would be required. If asbestos
does not require an export permit, it is one of the few things, as far as I know', that do not. The minister says it is in ample supply. It is not in ample supply, or these companies could get it. They are willing to pay more than the market price for it, but the big supplying companies will not give it, or they have failed to give it so far.
The minister evades altogether one of the most important features of this matter, and that is increasing the supply of building materials in the country. He evades altogether the point with respect to the loss of United States dollars. He tries to circumvent it by saying: You are a free enterprise party; why don't you write a letter to the man yourself? That answer is ridiculous, and I am surprised that the minister makes it. It is a disgrace that this situation continues, and the minister will take no action to correct it. Instead, he tries to make anyone bringing up the question appear ridiculous.

It was I who suggested to you, Mr. Chairman, that the committee be allowed wide latitude, and you kindly agreed. I think hon. members have availed themselves of it and brought out a good deal of information. Many of us will not be here on Monday, and there were one or two items-
Where are you going?

There are eighty-two
members who should be here from Ontario who will not be here. We have to go home to vote. If, Mr. Chairman, you think now, and the committee is agreeable, that the first item be called-

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister would give me a better answer than he has given as far as asbestos is concerned. So far he has given me no answer at all, I wonder if he will not give some reasonable answer on the matter. Surely I am entitled to an answer which is reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I wish my hon. friend would explain to me what branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce exercises the function that he has asked me to exercise. Under what authority w'ould I do it?
I just asked the minister if his department does not issue export permits.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We do on certain commodities.

Then the remedy is simple. It is right in the minister's hands. There is no difficulty about it as far as I can see.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Is my hon. friend suggesting that we place asbestos under export control, when we are using less than five per cent of our own production?

I am suggesting that the minister should request these firms to meet domestic requirements before they export all the asbestos from the country. They are exporting 96J per cent, I think it is, or they did last year, 1947. Surely they could afford to export only 95 per cent and supply Canadian requirements. I just cannot see where there would be any great hardship on the minister if he were asked to put a little pressure on those companies with a view to getting them to supply Canadian requirements first. That is all that is needed. If that fails I would suggest that he put on export control and look after the matter in that way.

The hon. member for Calgary West was asking for some information with respect to the values of the exports of Canadian goods to the devastated nations of Europe that might be expected under ERP. The minister has not given us any answers, but some figures have been given in the press. I should like the minister, if he would, to do us the honour of commenting on those figures. This was what was said in the daily press of May 14 last:
In the case of base metals and timber the Washington blueprint has given Canada a substantial share of the European requirement. There is some doubt whether this country will actually be able to supply the $157 million in timber. The United States allotment is $96 million. This country will also be expected to supply the largest bulk of the aluminum and newsprint.
I am simply referring to the fact that it is said here that the requirements which 'will be expected of Canada in respect of timber will be $157 million. A little further on, the article goes on to say:
Total allotment for fish in the Washington plan is $40 million, of which Canada is to supply only $12 million.
I wish to ask the minister whether those figures are definite, or if they are near the mark. If they are the estimates that have been in the plan, will he please give us some idea of what actually may be expected to come out of this plan?
I notice that the minister-and I referred to this a while ago-said in his speech at Montreal that this plan would involve some sacrifices here in Canada. The comment in the press is this:
There will be an attempt encouraged by Washington to obtain more and more exchange of goods between soft currency countries.

The United Kingdom has already gone quite a step in this direction and as her prodnetive capacity increases she is likely more and more to shut out Canadian markets in Europe for manufactured goods. This applies, too, to some basic food products.
If that is the sacrifice the minister is talking about, I wish he would give us some idea of what he means is the burden which would be placed upon us here and which we are expected to take our part in bearing.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Perhaps I can illustrate by using lumber as an example. We sell all the lumber we can produce. We have been doing that; we are doing it, and we expect to continue to do it. We get paid for that in dollars. Is it important where it goes?

It is important, I suppose, if all our lumber is taken. That is the point I am trying to get at. Are we making sacrifices by giving what we really can not afford to give? If we give our full supply, of course we are doing ourselves a great injustice.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
No. We have a certain export quota for lumber. It is something like sixty or sixty-five per cent of our total output, That is all	sold	for dollars. We	sell	all	the aluminum	that	we can produce	and	we	sell it fordollars. I	have mentioned	fish	as	a difficultitem.	As	I said in Montreal,	and my hon.
friend has quoted me, one of the rules of ERP is that soft currency countries must buy all they can from other soft currency countries. These soft currency countries produce a great deal of fish. We have been selling our fish as food and have been selling it mostly in Europe. It may be difficult, to sell that fish in the future. In other words, the fish people may have to make sacrifices beyond what they have had to make in the past. I am thinking of an item like fountain pens, and I do not know why I choose them. We have been selling fountain pens to Europe and to soft currency countries and charging up the price against the loan. I doubt very much if fountain pens would qualify under ERP, although I am not sure. Suppose they did not.
What about manufactured goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That would be a sacrifice for the fountain pen manufacturers. It is articles of that type to which I was referring. The point I am making is that we believe the general level of our exports will stay above that of last year, and payment will be made in dollars.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall the
item carry?

Supply-Trade and Commerce

No. I still have not had an. answer from the minister saying what he is prepared to do on the asbestos matter. As far as I am concerned, there is no use in his trying to laugh it off or to do anything else along that line. I want an answer that is definite either one way or the other; I want him to say either that he will or that he will not do anything. If he will not do anything, let him say so. If he is prepared to do anything, I should like to hear what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If my hon. friend wants me to use my influence, I suppose as a politician or a public man or something-
As Minister of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: -to do something for somebody in his constituency which I have no right to do under any powers entrusted to me, I do not chose to do it.

I said that there were two companies here, one in Calgary and one in Vancouver, which are making building supplies. I thought the minister was interested in getting an increase in building supplies. That is what I am interested in. I am not interested in his using his influence on behalf of one of my constituents. As a matter of fact, the people in this concern, as far as I know, are not my constituents.
No; they are mine.

Yes. I do not think they are in my constituency at all. Answers along that line are indicative of the fact that the minister is apparently not prepared to do the things which I think it is his duty to do as Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Carried.
No, no. Do not start calling "carried." As a matter of fact, I am prepared to talk here all night and all day tomorrow on this thing, until I get some satisfaction.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members can call "carried" as much as they like, but this is a serious matter. It is a matter which affects the employment of a considerable number of people in both those cities, who work in these plants. It is a matter which affects the number of buildings which can be put up and completed in those two cities and areas. If the minister has any real interest in that sort of thing, I should think he would take the necessary means to see to it that the small amount of asbestos fibre which they require
is retained in this country. I have suggested to him two things that he might do. He is apparently not prepared to do either of them. I really cannot understand the minister's attitude in the matter. To me he appears to be obstinate with regard to this matter and attempts to turn off any responsibility by answers which are not serious. That is what it amounts to.
Carried.

I have learned that I have a new constituent, Mr. Chairman.
I am going to put it in this way. We have items that are in short supply, such as nails, though I am not going to try to take the place of the hon. member for Peterborough West. We do exercise controls, some of them obvious and others not so obvious. May I ask, is there any import restriction or duty on asbestos fibre?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Not at all; it is duty free. Canada is the principal supplier.

Then, where may asbestos fibre be purchased other than from these plants in this part of the country? It cannot be purchased anywhere else in Canada and, as far as I know, it cannot be purchased in quantity in the United States. The minister turns this back; and a lot of the boys applauded his very clever reply when he said: You belong to a free enterprise party; why don't you write them a letter? We do belong to a free enterprise party; but we have always said that when monopoly raises its ugly head, as it has here, we will take care of it. That is what we are suggesting to the minister, who also says he belongs to a free enterprise party. He has it in his power to handle this situation, but all he is doing in his replies to those people who are trying to start a business, to provide some employment and to furnish some necessary materials, is passing them off with a smart answer and giving them no help whatever; while in this same Canada-and if we are to make it a Canada we have to trade within our own country as much as we can-we have the asbestos fibre. Out there we have the plants, but the minister will not do a single thing to help them. Nor is he even sympathetic toward these people in the difficulty in which they find themselves. That is the simple position of the Minister of Trade and Commerce right now in this House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Well, let us examine this situation a little further.

Yes, I think we had better.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend is suggesting that we have several producers of asbestos in this country who have combined to prevent a plant in Calgary from getting asbestos.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That is my hon. friend's statement. Well, we have Mr. F. A. McGregor as head of the combines investigation branch-
I did not say that and I ask the minister to withdraw that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: You said they just did not choose to sell asbestos to this plant. My hon. friend said they were trying to put the plant out of business so their United States associates could supply the finished product.
I never said that either.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Then your colleague from Calgary East said it.

No, I did not. I said these firms have never absolutely refused to sell asbestos to these people. They just keep giving them the run-around by shipping them asbestos in dribs and drabs every now and then, and never enough to meet their requirements.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Did my hon. friend not make the statement that a combine is raising its ugly head?
No; I said a monopoly was raising its ugly head; and I repeat it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is the same thing, if you are speaking of several firms.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Not while I am on my feet, surely.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I thought the hon. member had resumed his seat.
I had not, but I shall.

I should like to ask the minister to make another speech now on one of the other matters I asked him about before six o'clock. At the time the import restrictions and excise taxes were put on, or while they were being debated in the house, much was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance about the constructive side of the program for the conservation of United States dollars. I might just start the minister off by a reference

to his statement that if Canadians made the building up of United States dollar exports a national objective we should be able to balance our. trade in a matter of months. I think the committee would be interested to hear a statement by the minister as to what progress has been made with the constructive side of the dollar conservation program, how far he has gone with it and what mechanisms he has used to further this drive toward this national objective, also what he proposes to do in future to make it a reality' so that the restrictive side may be abandoned.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, the constructive side is showing itself in the trade figures. I could give my hon. friend details, but, without doing that, I can say the exports to dollar countries are stepping up each month in spectacular fashion, while imports from dollar countries are dropping each month in comparison with the same month last year. Exports are being stimulated by a formula worked! out particularly for plants using United States content. We are limiting the United States dollars that may be spent to a fraction of what was spent last year, but allow the plant to earn additional United States dollars to pay for imports by increasing exports. The result of that program has been quite spectacular, particularly in certain industries. Several industries have arranged to manufacture and ship into the United States market in a manner never contemplated before the program was put into effect. The over-all net result is that without counting loans, I believe we are about $150 million better off in our United States dbllar balance than we were when the program was announced, which I think is the best proof that can be offered that the constructive side is operating.
The minister mentions S150 million without including the loan. Will he say how much of that was the import of capital and how much was earned through increased export trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Obviously I have not the details on the balance of payments. The investment figures would be included in the amount I gave, but I doubt very much if the investments count very much one way or the other. They were moving against us for a time; probably they about balance now. We are over $100 million better off in our trade with the United States than we were at this time last year.

As I understand it, the minister has given us only one mechanism he has employed, namely, by giving firms which can export an additional quota of United

Supply-Trade and Commerce
States dollars so that they can buy goods to remanufacture. Does that represent the total government influence on the positive side of this program? Is the minister not following any other policy to stimulate those exports? For instance, it is suggested in the Financial Post of recent date that the government has in mind a much wider reciprocal trade deal with the United States. The particular passage I have before me goes so far as to say: "The next step unofficially announced as government policy is to negotiate a much wider reciprocal trade deal with the United States directly." I should have thought there would be something more than relief from one of the restrictions as the positive side of this policy. I would ask the minister to comment on what I have said, and to say what is proposed for the future, if he has anything in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Duties are adjusted from time to time. There have been reductions on base metals going into the United States. Nothing in the nature of a reciprocal deal has been worked out, but we are stimulating trade where we can, and stimulating exports where we can. I mentioned aluminum. A very large contract was made by the Aluminum Company of Canada to supply aluminum for the United States. Our nickel companies have large contracts with the United States. Both nickel companies are expanding their production in an endeavour to meet contracts that have been made in the United States within recent months. The point is that we are stimulating exports wherever we can and bv whatever means. Our program for curtailing imports is v'orking fairly well, and a combination of the two is producing United States dollars and is tending to pull us out of our balance of payment difficulty with the United States.
I understand that the minister could attempt to stimulate exports by exhorting the Canadian businessman to try to channel his trade that way-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We have not attempted to channel trade. Our efforts have been directed to obtaining more exports.
To the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: To anywhere; it is all the same.

The minister might appeal to the Canadian businessman, and I would approve that, to try to find sources of raw materials in Canada which had previously been imported; but I have not heard the minister
say anything about any concrete government policy that he has adopted as part of a positive program. I remember when he was stimulating building materials he had the idea of double depreciation to those who increased the size of their plants producing bathtubs and things like that. Is the government taking any steps, by way of fiscal policy, if you like to call it that, to induce Canadian manufacturers to develop Canadian sources of supply or to set up new industries to supply wants which previously were supplied by other countries? Is there no thought of some definite government policy which would be of assistance in getting additional exports, or is it simply a matter of calling the seriousness of the situation to the attention of Canadian businessmen and hoping that they will, as they probably will, do a good job? Has the minister the details of any specific things the government has done?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If my hon. friend will examine the act under which we work he will notice that we have the power to say whether a man can have his source of supply in this country or whether he may import his raw materials or semi-finished parts. We are using that power actively. A man must show good reason why he should import before he is given an import permit. If it is possible to get what he wants in Canada he is required to do so. Naturally the demand for new products is causing new plants to open. There has been a great expansion of parts manufacturing in the country, and expansion is still continuing. Firms which are large importers are constantly looking for new sources of supply.
It really comes down to this. The minister is using his restrictive program to try to stimulate a productive program.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Certainly.
That is the extent to which there is a positive program?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I wish my hon. friend would not put words into my mouth.
I was just asking the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I have given several examples of what we are doing. We are finding new markets; we are inducing shippers to find new markets and we are aiding them in every way. The point I make is that it is working. I think that is disappointing to my hon. friend, because it was freely predicted that the program would not work. But it is working;
4834

Supply-Trade and Commerce
we hope it will continue to work, and we believe that we shall be out of the restrictive phase in a foreseeable time.
A matter of months.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There have not been so many months. When my hon. friend says there is only one way, I tell him that we are acting in many ways.

Of course the minister is quite wrong in stating that I would be disappointed if he were not successful. As a matter of fact, I would be most delighted if he were successful. I will say to him that from the beginning of the session in December we on this side were sceptical as to whether there was a positive side to the government's program to conserve United States dollars. We heard vague references made in speeches of the Minister of Finance and of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the constructive side of the program, but we have never seen it in concrete form. I was giving the minister an opportunity to let the committee know what the concrete form of this constructive policy is.
I have asked the minister these questions, but he could have avoided any questions from me by making a statement on the matter. I think I was pretty close to giving a fair summary of the whole constructive policy in the conservation of United States dollars when I said that it sounded to me like being simply the use of import restriction measures to try to stimulate production in other ways. I think we see tonight that the government have no constructive policy for the building up of our United States exchange reserve and that our suspicions right from the beginning of the session that it was just a figure of speech are borne out.

Let me deal with the same subject in another way. In January, 1947, the Department of Trade and Commerce put out a booklet on foreign trade, a copy of which I hold in my hand. That received a fine reception from industrialists and manufacturers and exporters throughout Canada. I sent out quite a number of them to industries in my district and received some nice replies. However I think I should pass on to the minister one reply that I received.
They said there were a lot of pictures of commissioners, a lot of pictures of commodities and pictures of other parts of the world, but they wanted to know if it should not go a great deal farther. They wanted to know whether these commissioners in the various parts of the world should not be doing more to see that

their products were being sold in the countries in which they were located. That presents the other side of this control business.
As the minister said a while ago, one principle of ERP is that soft currency countries should trade among themselves; in other words, they should pull themselves up by their own boot-straps, that they should go into production themselves. We in Canada, not having our full share of United States dollars, should as much as possible trade with those countries and trade would thereby be stimulated. However we cannot get into a number of the sterling area countries which are dependencies and dominions of the United Kingdom, because they have import controls similar to our own.
The suggestion has been made by industrialists that our trade commissioners in sterling area countries should busy themselves to expedite the negotiation of reciprocal trade arrangements. The minister has stated that the principle of ERP is to expand trade among countries which cannot otherwise help themselves; and I should like to know what, if anything, has been or can be done by Canada to work out reciprocal trade conventions with those countries which have shut their doors to our products.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not know what my hon. friend understands by reciprocal trade agreements. AVe are a party to multilateral trade agreements worked out at Geneva.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Canada barters frequently. Canadian firms barter with firms abroad.

I suggest that the Department of Trade and Commerce, who are in this thing up to their neck, ought, through their trade commissioners, to perform greater service, because whatever stimulus can be given to our trade will help us to get away from controls all the faster.
